questions.question: Which of the following analyses is qualitative only?
questions.answer: Detecting whether strontium ions are present is a qualitative test (presence or absence). The other options all measure an amount (C).
options: Analysis of the blood alcohol content of a motorist.
Measurement of the acid content of orange juice.
Detection of strontium ions in polluted water.
Use of gravimetric analysis to determine the molar mass of an organic compound.

questions.question: Bromine water can be used in the school laboratory to distinguish between which of the following types of organic compounds.
questions.answer: Bromine water is decolourised by an alkene (addition across C=C) but not by an alkane. Both alkenes and alkynes decolourise it, so A is wrong, and the others do not react (B).

questions.question: How can dynamic chemical equilibrium best be described?
questions.answer: Dynamic equilibrium requires a closed system, in which the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates (so concentrations are constant) (B). The reactions do not cease.
options: An open system in which the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.
A closed system in which the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.
A closed system in which all reactions have ceased and so concentrations of all species remain constant.
An open system in which all reactions have ceased and so concentrations of all species remain constant.

questions.question: Which of the following is a limitation of the Brønsted-Lowry theory of acids?
questions.answer: The Brønsted–Lowry theory defines acids as proton donors, so it cannot account for acid–base behaviour that does not involve proton transfer (e.g. $SO_3+CaO\rightarrow CaSO_4$ or $BF_3+NH_3$), which the Lewis theory explains (D).
options: The theory did not classify HCl as an acid.
The theory cannot explain non-neutral salt solutions.
The theory cannot explain neutralisation reactions in non-aqueous solvents.
The theory cannot explain neutralisation reactions where proton transfer does not occur.

questions.question: The basic principle behind the analysis of compounds using infrared spectroscopy is the
questions.answer: Infrared radiation is absorbed at frequencies that match the stretching and bending vibrations of covalent bonds (D). B describes UV–visible spectroscopy and C describes NMR.
options: movement of electrons in the molecule.
movement of electrons between different energy levels.
absorption of radiation by nuclei placed in a magnetic field.
bending or stretching vibrations of covalent bonds in molecules.

questions.question: To prepare a series of standards for the calibration of an atomic absorption spectrometer a stock solution of 0.100 M nickel(II) sulfate was required. To prepare the stock solution
questions.answer: $n=0.100\times0.5000=0.0500$ mol and $m=0.0500\times154.75=7.74$ g. A standard solution must be made up to the calibration mark in a volumetric flask after dissolving the solid in a small volume of water (C).
options: 15.5 g of $NiSO_4$ should be dissolved in 500.0 mL of distilled water in a beaker.
7.74 g of $NiSO_4$ should be added to 500.0 mL of distilled water in a volumetric flask.
7.74 g of $NiSO_4$ should be transferred to a 500.0 mL volumetric flask, the solid dissolved in a small volume of distilled water and the volume made up to the calibration mark with distilled water.
15.5 g of $NiSO_4$ should be transferred to a 500.0 mL volumetric flask, the solid dissolved in a small volume of distilled water and the volume made up to the calibration mark with distilled water.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a conjugate acid-base pair?
questions.answer: A conjugate pair differs by one proton. $H_3O^+$ and $OH^-$ differ by two protons (the conjugate base of $H_3O^+$ is $H_2O$) (B).

questions.question: What is the correct IUPAC name for the compound with the structural formula shown below?
questions.answer: The OH group has priority for numbering, so it takes the lowest locant (carbon 2), which puts the halogens on carbon 5. The substituents are listed alphabetically: chloro before fluoro, giving 5-chloro-5-fluoropentan-2-ol (C).

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT have an isomer?
questions.answer: Ethene ($C_2H_4$) has no isomers. Pentane has 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane, but-1-ene has but-2-ene and cyclobutane, and cyclopropane is an isomer of propene (A).

questions.question: 20.00 mL of 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$ of a strong diprotic acid was diluted to 250.0 mL with distilled water. What was the pH of the final solution?
questions.answer: $n(acid)=0.02000\times0.10=2.0\times10^{-3}$ mol, which gives $4.0\times10^{-3}$ mol of $H^+$ (strong diprotic acid). $[H^+]=\dfrac{4.0\times10^{-3}}{0.2500}=0.016$ M, so pH $=-\log(0.016)=1.8$ (C).

questions.question: In which solution will $PbI_2$ have the lowest molar solubility? $PbI_2(s)\rightleftharpoons Pb^{2+}(aq)+2I^-(aq)$, $K_{sp}=9.8\times10^{-9}$
questions.answer: Solubility is lowest where the common-ion concentration is greatest, with $K_{sp}=[Pb^{2+}][I^-]^2$. In 0.02 M KI, $[I^-]=0.02$ M: $s=\dfrac{9.8\times10^{-9}}{(0.02)^2}=2.5\times10^{-5}$ M. In 0.02 M $CaI_2$, $[I^-]=0.04$ M: $s=\dfrac{9.8\times10^{-9}}{(0.04)^2}=6.1\times10^{-6}$ M. In 0.02 M $Pb^{2+}$ solutions: $s=\dfrac12\sqrt{K_{sp}/0.02}\approx3.5\times10^{-4}$ M. $CaI_2$ gives the lowest (B).

questions.question: The mass spectrum for pentane is shown below. Which of the following ions would most likely give rise to the base peak (m/z 43) in this spectrum?
questions.answer: The base peak at m/z 43 corresponds to $C_3H_7^+$ ($3\times12+7=43$), the propyl cation $CH_3CH_2CH_2^+$ (C). It forms by simple cleavage of a C–C bond in the straight chain pentane molecular ion. Option A is $C_2H_5^+$ (m/z 29), B is the branched isopropyl cation (also m/z 43, but it would require rearrangement of the straight chain), and D is the molecular ion (m/z 72).

questions.question: A student weighed out 2.5 g of fertiliser, dissolved it in water and added 150.0 mL of 0.25 M barium chloride solution. The precipitate of barium sulfate, after being filtered off and dried to constant mass, weighed 3.8 g. What was the percentage by mass of sulfate in the fertiliser?

Which of the following alcohols have been classified correctly?

| | Primary | Secondary | Tertiary |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | butan-1-ol | 2-methylpropan-1-ol | 2-methylpropan-2-ol |
| B | propan-1-ol | pentan-3-ol | 2-methylpropan-2-ol |
| C | 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol | butan-2-ol | ethanol |
| D | propan-2-ol | butan-2-ol | pentan-3-ol |
questions.answer: Propan-1-ol is primary, pentan-3-ol is secondary and 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary (B). In A, 2-methylpropan-1-ol is primary, not secondary. In C, ethanol is primary. In D, propan-2-ol is secondary and pentan-3-ol is secondary.

questions.question: Which is the INCORRECT statement about the reaction when solid magnesium burns in air?
questions.answer: $2Mg(s)+O_2(g)\rightarrow2MgO(s)$ is a combustion with $\Delta H<0$. A gas is consumed to form a solid, so entropy decreases ($\Delta S<0$). Statement C (entropy change positive) is incorrect. The reaction goes to completion in an open system, so D is correct (C).
options: The reaction is described as combustion.
The enthalpy and entropy changes for the reaction are both negative.
The enthalpy change is negative while the change in entropy is positive.
The reaction does not reach equilibrium and the system is classified as open.

questions.question: When pent-1-ene undergoes an addition reaction with water, two products are formed (pentan-1-ol and pentan-2-ol). Which of the following alkenes will also produce two products when they undergo an addition reaction with water?
questions.answer: Two products form when the double bond is unsymmetrical, so OH can add to either carbon of the double bond to give different alcohols. Oct-2-ene gives octan-2-ol and octan-3-ol (C). Ethene, but-2-ene and hex-3-ene are symmetrical and give a single product each.

questions.question: Sulfur trioxide is produced by the reaction of sulfur dioxide with oxygen: $2SO_2(g)+O_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2SO_3(g)$. 8.0 mol of $SO_2(g)$ was placed in a 2.0 L container with 4.0 mol of $O_2(g)$ and allowed to reach equilibrium. At equilibrium, the concentration of $SO_3(g)$ was 2.0 mol L$^{-1}$. What is the value of $K_{eq}$ under these conditions?

The following concentration–time graph refers to a mixture of three gases, P, Q and R, in an enclosed 5.0 L container. At time T the mixture is heated. The equilibrium system that represents the graph is
questions.answer: After heating, [P] rises by 0.25 M while [Q] falls by 0.5 M and [R] falls by 0.25 M. So $2Q+R\rightarrow P$ is the direction of the shift, in the ratio 2 : 1 : 1, i.e. the equilibrium is $P\rightleftharpoons2Q+R$. Heating favours the endothermic direction, which is therefore the reverse reaction, so the forward reaction is exothermic (A).
options: $P(g)\rightleftharpoons2Q(g)+R(g)$ and the forward reaction is exothermic.
$2Q(g)\rightleftharpoons P(g)+R(g)$ and the forward reaction is endothermic.
$2Q(g)+R(g)\rightleftharpoons P(g)$ and the forward reaction is exothermic.
$P(g)+2Q(g)\rightleftharpoons R(g)$ and the forward reaction is endothermic.

questions.question: An aqueous solution of sodium dihydrogen phosphate ($NaH_2PO_4$) has a pH less than 7 due to the following equilibrium being established in solution: $H_2PO_4^-(aq)+H_2O(l)\rightleftharpoons HPO_4^{2-}(aq)+H_3O^+(aq)$. Which statement best explains this observation?
questions.answer: The solution is acidic because $H_2PO_4^-$ donates a proton to water (producing $H_3O^+$) more than it accepts one: water is a stronger base than $H_2PO_4^-$ (B). $H_2PO_4^-$ is a weak acid, so A is wrong.
options: The conjugate base of $H_2PO_4^-(aq)$ is a stronger base than $H_2O(l)$.

questions.question: When 0.150 M HCl(aq) was added to a 20.0 mL sample of aqueous $Ba(OH)_2(aq)$, it generated the titration curve shown as a solid line. If the same number of moles of $Ba(OH)_2$, but initially at a volume of 10.0 mL, were titrated with 0.150 M HCl, which of the dotted line curves would best describe this new titration?
questions.answer: The same moles of base need the same volume of 0.150 M HCl, so the equivalence point is at the same volume as before (this eliminates A and C). The $Ba(OH)_2$ is now twice as concentrated, so the initial pH is slightly higher (by about 0.3), and the final solution is less dilute so the final pH is slightly lower. The dotted curve starts a little above and finishes a little below the solid curve, with the same equivalence volume (B).

questions.question: Consider the following equilibrium system. $Fe^{3+}(aq)+SCN^-(aq)\rightleftharpoons[FeNCS]^{2+}(aq)$ ($\Delta H<0$; yellow, colourless, blood-red). The solution is blood-red. On addition of 1.0 M KOH(aq) to the equilibrium system, the blood-red colour of the solution faded and $Fe(OH)_3(s)$ formed as a brown precipitate. Explain the colour change of the solution in terms of collision theory and rate of reaction.
questions.answer: The brown $Fe(OH)_3(s)$ precipitate removes $Fe^{3+}$ ions from solution. As a result the frequency of collisions between reactant particles decreases, and the rate of the forward reaction decreases. The removal of $Fe^{3+}$ does not change the frequency of collisions between product particles, so the rate of the reverse reaction initially remains constant, and is now greater than the forward reaction rate. The equilibrium therefore shifts left, the concentration of $[FeNCS]^{2+}$ decreases and the blood-red colour fades.

questions.question: Justify ONE way to shift the equilibrium $Fe^{3+}+SCN^-\rightleftharpoons[FeNCS]^{2+}$ ($\Delta H<0$) to the right, without adding any further reagents to the equilibrium system.
questions.answer: Cool the system (decrease the temperature). The forward reaction is exothermic ($\Delta H<0$), so by Le Châtelier's principle a decrease in temperature favours the reaction that produces heat, the forward reaction, shifting the equilibrium to the right.

questions.question: The Australian health guideline for lead in garden soil is no more than 300 mg/kg. Lead is a neurotoxin that affects childhood development. A sample of soil was suspected of containing high levels of lead. To determine the concentration of lead in the soil, atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) was used with an appropriate lamp with a wavelength of 218 nm. The graph shows the calibration of absorbance against concentration of $Pb^{2+}$ (mg/L). A 2.00 g sample of the soil was taken and dissolved in acid and diluted to a total volume of 50.0 mL. The absorbance of the sample was determined to be 0.25. Using the graph, calculate the concentration of lead in the soil and determine if it is safe to grow vegetables.
questions.answer: From the calibration graph, an absorbance of 0.25 corresponds to $[Pb^{2+}]=3.7$ mg/L. Mass of lead in the 50.0 mL: $3.7\times0.0500=0.185$ mg. Mass of soil $=2.00\ \text{g}=0.00200$ kg. $$\text{concentration}=\frac{0.185}{0.00200}=92.5\ \text{mg/kg}\ (\approx93\ \text{mg/kg}).$$ This is below the guideline of 300 mg/kg, so the soil is safe for growing vegetables.

questions.question: A sequence of chemical reactions, starting with pent-2-ene, is shown in the flow chart (pent-2-ene +HCl(aq) → A; pent-2-ene +$H_2$, Ni catalyst → B; B → (Step C) 1-bromopentane → (Step D) pentan-1-ol → (hot concentrated $KMnO_4$/$H_2SO_4$) → E). Complete the flow chart by drawing structural formulae for compounds A, B and E.
questions.answer: **A:** 3-chloropentane, $CH_3CH_2CHClCH_2CH_3$ (2-chloropentane, $CH_3CHClCH_2CH_2CH_3$, is also a possible product). **B:** pentane, $CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_3$. **E:** pentanoic acid, $CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2COOH$ (pentanal is an intermediate in this oxidation).

questions.question: Complete the table to identify the reagent and conditions required at Steps C (pentane to 1-bromopentane) and D (1-bromopentane to pentan-1-ol) in the flow chart above.
questions.answer:
| Step | Reagent | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| C | $Br_2$ (Br–Br) | UV light |
| D | $H_2O$ or NaOH(aq) | heat (ethanol as solvent) |

questions.question: If these reactions were carried out in the school laboratory, justify ONE precaution that would be needed.
questions.answer: Any one of: keep organic chemicals (e.g. pentane, pentanol) away from open flames and sparks because they are highly flammable; work in a fume cupboard or well-ventilated area because the fumes (and bromine) are toxic/harmful; wear gloves, goggles and a lab coat because bromine, acids and permanganate are corrosive.

questions.question: The graph below shows how the boiling point of two different straight chain homologous series, alkanes and alkanols, vary with number of carbon atoms. State and explain the trends in boiling point shown in the graph for both alkanes and alkanols.
questions.answer: For both series, the boiling point increases as the number of carbon atoms increases, because the longer chains have larger electron clouds, so there are stronger and more dispersion forces which require more energy to break. At each number of carbon atoms the alkanol has a higher boiling point than the alkane. Alkanes have only dispersion forces. Alkanols also have strong hydrogen bonding between the OH groups (in addition to dispersion forces), which requires much more energy to overcome.

questions.question:
The boiling points of various straight chain alkanoic acids are given in the table below. Graph this data on the grid to show how the boiling points of alkanoic acids compare with the other two homologous series.

| Carbon atoms | Boiling point (°C) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 101 |
| 2 | 118 |
| 3 | 141 |
| 4 | 164 |
| 5 | 186 |
| 6 | 205 |
| 7 | 223 |
| 8 | 239 |
| 9 | 259 |
questions.answer: Plot each point (number of carbon atoms on the x-axis, boiling point on the y-axis) and draw a smooth line of best fit through the points. The alkanoic acid line lies above the alkanol line (and well above the alkane line) at every carbon number, with a similar upward trend.

questions.question: Explain why your graph for alkanoic acids sits above that of alkanols.
questions.answer: Alkanoic acids have a carboxyl group (C=O and O–H). In addition to dispersion forces, they form hydrogen bonds through the OH group and have dipole–dipole forces due to the polar carbonyl group. They can also form hydrogen-bonded dimers. This gives stronger intermolecular forces than in alkanols (which have only hydrogen bonding and dispersion forces), so more energy is needed to separate the molecules and the boiling points are higher.

questions.question: During an outdoor school camp, a group of students used a cooking stove that is fuelled with liquid butane cylinders. The cooking stove was used to heat a kettle containing 950 mL of water at 12 °C. Calculate the mass of butane required to heat the water to its boiling point given that only 40% of the energy provided by the combustion reaction of butane actually goes to heating the water. The enthalpy of combustion of butane is $-2878\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
questions.answer: $m(H_2O)=950$ g, $\Delta T=100-12=88$ °C: $q=mc\Delta T=950\times4.18\times88=3.49\times10^5$ J $=349.4$ kJ (only 40% of the energy released). Energy released by combustion $=\dfrac{349.4}{0.40}=873.6$ kJ. $n(C_4H_{10})=\dfrac{873.6}{2878}=0.3035$ mol. $$m=nM=0.3035\times58.12=17.6\ \text{g}\approx18\ \text{g}.$$

questions.question: Describe TWO environmental implications of using hydrocarbons like butane.
questions.answer: Any two of: combustion releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, contributing to global warming and ocean acidification (and oxides such as NO, $NO_2$ and $SO_2$ cause air pollution and acid rain); hydrocarbons are non-renewable fossil fuel resources that are being depleted; extraction (mining, drilling) damages land, soil and habitats and can cause pollution or accidents such as oil spills; plastics made from hydrocarbons are non-biodegradable and cause pollution.

questions.question: Three solutions of equal concentration of sodium nitrate, ammonium nitrate and sodium propanoate were prepared, and their pH values were measured. List the solutions in order from lowest to highest pH.
questions.answer: Ammonium nitrate (lowest pH), sodium nitrate, sodium propanoate (highest pH).

questions.question: Three solutions of equal concentration of sodium nitrate, ammonium nitrate and sodium propanoate were prepared, and their pH values were measured. Using your knowledge of acids and bases, justify the order given in part (a).
questions.answer: **Ammonium nitrate (lowest pH, acidic):** $NH_4^+$ is the conjugate acid of the weak base $NH_3$, so it donates a proton to water: $NH_4^++H_2O\rightleftharpoons NH_3+H_3O^+$, giving pH < 7; $NO_3^-$ is the conjugate base of a strong acid and does not react. **Sodium nitrate (neutral):** both $Na^+$ and $NO_3^-$ are conjugates of a strong base and a strong acid, with no tendency to react with water, so pH $\approx7$. **Sodium propanoate (highest pH, basic):** the propanoate ion is the conjugate base of the weak acid propanoic acid, so it accepts a proton from water: $CH_3CH_2COO^-+H_2O\rightleftharpoons CH_3CH_2COOH+OH^-$, giving pH > 7.

questions.question: A trainee analytical chemist was given a sample of river water, contaminated with a single metal ion from barium, calcium, magnesium, lead or silver. She (1) gently boiled 500 mL of the water down to 10 mL to increase the concentration, (2) measured three separate 1 mL samples, and (3) added 3 drops of each reagent to the concentrated water. Test 1, 1 M NaOH: white precipitate. Test 2, 1 M $H_2SO_4$: white precipitate. Test 3, 1 M NaCl: no reaction. The trainee reported that the water was contaminated with calcium ions. Evaluate the validity of the procedure AND the conclusion made by the trainee analytical chemist. Include a net ionic equation for the formation of one of the possible precipitates.
questions.answer: **Procedure:** concentrating the sample by boiling is valid and useful, because low ion concentrations may fail to give a precipitate (e.g. calcium sulfate is only sparingly soluble). Using separate samples for each test is also good. However the procedure cannot identify a single ion. **Test 1 (NaOH):** silver would give a brown precipitate ($Ag_2O$), so silver is eliminated, but $Ca^{2+}$, $Mg^{2+}$, $Pb^{2+}$ and $Ba^{2+}$ can all give white hydroxide precipitates (barium hydroxide is slightly soluble). **Test 2 ($H_2SO_4$):** barium, calcium, lead and silver sulfates are white precipitates, but magnesium sulfate is soluble, so magnesium is eliminated. **Test 3 (NaCl):** no reaction rules out lead (and silver), because $PbCl_2$ and $AgCl$ would precipitate. $CaCl_2$ and $BaCl_2$ are soluble, so both calcium and barium remain possible. **Conclusion:** the tests eliminate Ag, Mg and Pb but cannot distinguish between Ca and Ba, so the conclusion that the ion is calcium is not justified (it is only possible, not valid). A further test (e.g. a flame test: calcium is brick-red, barium is pale green) is needed. Net ionic equation: $Ca^{2+}(aq)+SO_4^{2-}(aq)\rightarrow CaSO_4(s)$ (or $Ba^{2+}(aq)+SO_4^{2-}(aq)\rightarrow BaSO_4(s)$).

questions.question: The active ingredient in TUMS is calcium carbonate ($CaCO_3$). The following back titration procedure is used: 1. Add 1.30 g of finely ground tablet to a conical flask. 2. Pipette 25.00 mL of 1.073 M hydrochloric acid into the flask. 3. Stir for 5 minutes. 4. Add 10 mL of 1 M sodium phosphate (to remove calcium ions). 5. Heat gently with stirring for 10 minutes. 6. Titrate with 1.102 M sodium hydroxide using a conductivity probe. The average data from the conductometric titration is shown on the graph. The manufacturer states that the quantity of calcium carbonate in each tablet should be between 38–40% by mass, calculated using % mass $CaCO_3=\dfrac{\text{mass }CaCO_3}{\text{mass tablet}}\times100\%$. Assess whether this batch of TUMS tablets is within the specified range.
questions.answer: From the graph, the equivalence point (the minimum conductivity, where the two lines intersect) is at $V(NaOH)=15.00$ mL. $n(NaOH)=1.102\times0.01500=0.01653$ mol, and since $HCl+NaOH\rightarrow NaCl+H_2O$ is 1:1, $n(HCl)_{excess}=0.01653$ mol. $n(HCl)_{total}=1.073\times0.02500=0.026825$ mol. $n(HCl)_{reacted}=0.026825-0.01653=0.010295$ mol. $CaCO_3+2HCl\rightarrow CaCl_2+CO_2+H_2O$, so $n(CaCO_3)=\dfrac{0.010295}{2}=5.1475\times10^{-3}$ mol and $m=5.1475\times10^{-3}\times100.09=0.5152$ g. $$\%\ CaCO_3=\frac{0.5152}{1.30}\times100=39.6\%.$$ This is between 38% and 40%, so the batch is within the specified range. (The school's sample answer gave 39.8%, a rounding slip; the correct value is 39.6%, which does not change the conclusion.)

questions.question: When calcium carbonate is neutralised by hydrochloric acid some of the carbon dioxide gas produced dissolves in the solution. This results in the formation of carbonic acid, $H_2CO_3(aq)$, as shown below: $CO_2(g)\rightleftharpoons CO_2(aq)$, $\Delta H<0$; $CO_2(aq)+H_2O(l)\rightleftharpoons H_2CO_3(aq)$, $\Delta H<0$, $K_{eq}=3.1\times10^{-5}$ at 25 °C. Using this information and your knowledge of equilibrium and titration, evaluate the importance of Step 5 (heating gently with stirring for 10 minutes) in terms of the accuracy of the quality control analysis.
questions.answer: Both equilibria are exothermic in the forward direction, so heating shifts them to the left, driving dissolved $CO_2$ out of solution and removing carbonic acid. If carbonic acid remained, it would add extra $H^+$ (as a weak acid) that would be neutralised by the NaOH in Step 6. This increases the volume of NaOH required and gives an overestimate of the excess HCl, hence the amount of HCl that reacted with $CaCO_3$ and the % mass of $CaCO_3$ would be underestimated. Step 5 is therefore important for the accuracy of the analysis.

questions.question: Carbon, as graphite, burns to form gaseous carbon dioxide. Thermodynamic data (at 298 K) for the complete combustion of graphite: $\Delta_cH^\circ=-393.5\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, $\Delta_cS^\circ=2.9\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$. Calculate $\Delta_cG^\circ$ in kJ mol$^{-1}$.
questions.answer: $\Delta G^\circ=\Delta H^\circ-T\Delta S^\circ=-393.5-(298)(2.9\times10^{-3})=-394.4\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\ (\approx-390\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\ \text{to 2 s.f.})$

questions.question: Use this data to explain why the combustion of graphite does not come to equilibrium but instead will always proceed to completion irrespective of the temperature at which the reaction takes place.
questions.answer: Equilibrium requires $\Delta G\approx0$. Here $\Delta G$ is large and negative, so the reaction does not reach an equilibrium mixture but goes to completion. $\Delta H$ is negative and $\Delta S$ is positive (a gas is formed from a solid), so $-T\Delta S$ is also negative at every temperature. Therefore $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S$ is always negative, whatever the temperature, so the reaction always proceeds to completion.

questions.question: A clear colourless liquid is labelled 'C$_5$H$_{10}$O$_2$'. Chemical tests: bromine water, no reaction; acidified potassium permanganate, no reaction; sodium hydrogen carbonate, bubbles of gas produced. The infrared spectrum (strong peak near 1700 cm$^{-1}$ and a very broad absorption about 2500–3300 cm$^{-1}$), $^1$H NMR and $^{13}$C NMR spectra are shown. $^1$H NMR data: 0.9 ppm (area 6, doublet); 2.05 ppm (area 1, complex multiplet); 2.15 ppm (area 2, doublet); 11.0 ppm (area 1, singlet). Draw a structural formula for the organic compound, name the compound and justify your answer using relevant information from the chemical tests and each of the spectra.
questions.answer: **Compound: 3-methylbutanoic acid**, $(CH_3)_2CHCH_2COOH$. **Chemical tests:** no reaction with bromine water means no C=C bond (not an alkene); no reaction with acidified permanganate means it is not a primary or secondary alcohol or aldehyde; bubbles of gas with $NaHCO_3$ ($CO_2$) show it is a carboxylic acid. **IR:** a strong C=O absorption (about 1700–1750 cm$^{-1}$) and a very broad O–H absorption (2500–3300 cm$^{-1}$) are characteristic of a carboxylic acid. **$^{13}C$ NMR:** four signals for five carbons, so two carbons are equivalent: about 180 ppm (C=O of COOH), about 45 ppm (CH$_2$ next to the C=O), and two signals at about 23–25 ppm (the CH and the two equivalent CH$_3$ groups). **$^1H$ NMR:** 11.0 ppm, singlet, 1H: COOH. 2.15 ppm, doublet, 2H: $CH_2$ next to C=O, split by one neighbouring H (the CH). 2.05 ppm, multiplet, 1H: the CH, split by the $CH_2$ and six CH$_3$ hydrogens. 0.9 ppm, doublet, 6H: two equivalent $CH_3$ groups split by the one CH. Together these show a $CH(CH_3)_2$ group attached to a $CH_2$ next to the COOH.

questions.question: Draw and name a straight chain isomer of the organic compound you have identified in part (a) and compare the infrared spectrum for the isomer with that of the organic compound from the storeroom.
questions.answer: The straight-chain isomer is **pentanoic acid**, $CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2COOH$. **Similarity:** both are carboxylic acids, so both IR spectra show the same absorptions for the O–H (very broad, 2500–3300 cm$^{-1}$) and C=O (about 1700 cm$^{-1}$) bonds. **Difference:** the spectra would differ in the fingerprint region (below about 1500 cm$^{-1}$), where the pattern of peaks is unique to the structure (branched vs straight chain).

questions.question: A student slowly added a small mass of solid barium hydroxide to 100 mL of distilled water at 25 °C. The solution was stirred and the pH measured with a probe. 60 seconds after the addition, the student thought they observed a slight cloudiness in the solution and assumed the solution was saturated. The pH of the mixture at this time was 11.8. Use the data recorded by the student to determine if the solution was saturated at 60 seconds. Show your working.
questions.answer: $Ba(OH)_2(s)\rightleftharpoons Ba^{2+}(aq)+2OH^-(aq)$, $K_{sp}=2.55\times10^{-4}$. $pOH=14.0-11.8=2.2$, so $[OH^-]=10^{-2.2}=6.3\times10^{-3}$ M and $[Ba^{2+}]=\tfrac12[OH^-]=3.2\times10^{-3}$ M. $$Q_{sp}=[Ba^{2+}][OH^-]^2=(3.2\times10^{-3})(6.3\times10^{-3})^2=1.3\times10^{-7}.$$ Since $Q_{sp}<K_{sp}$ ($1.3\times10^{-7}<2.55\times10^{-4}$) the solution is **not saturated** at 60 seconds (the cloudiness was due to something else, such as undissolved solid or dissolved carbon dioxide forming barium carbonate).

questions.question: A student has four solutions: A, 50 mL 1.0 M sodium acetate; B, 50 mL 1.0 M acetic acid; C, 50 mL 0.5 M hydrochloric acid; D, 50 mL 0.5 M sodium hydroxide. When Solution A is mixed with Solution B a buffer is formed that has a pH of 4.74. Explain, without the use of calculations, why the pH only increases to 4.75 when 0.5 mL of 0.1 M sodium hydroxide is added to this buffer. Include a chemical equation in your answer.
questions.answer: The buffer has large and equal concentrations of acetic acid and acetate ions. The added hydroxide ions react with acetic acid: $$CH_3COOH(aq)+OH^-(aq)\rightarrow CH_3COO^-(aq)+H_2O(l)$$ Because the amount of acetic acid present is much larger than the amount of $OH^-$ added, almost all of the $OH^-$ is neutralised, the ratio $[CH_3COO^-]/[CH_3COOH]$ changes only slightly, and so the $[H_3O^+]$ and the pH stay close to their original value.

questions.question: Justify why a buffer can be prepared from a mixture of Solution B (50 mL 1.0 M acetic acid) and Solution D (50 mL 0.5 M sodium hydroxide) but not from a mixture of Solution B and Solution C (50 mL 0.5 M hydrochloric acid). Support your answer with a chemical equation.
questions.answer: B + D: $CH_3COOH+OH^-\rightarrow CH_3COO^-+H_2O$. The 0.025 mol of NaOH converts half of the 0.050 mol of acetic acid to acetate, giving relatively large and equal amounts of a weak acid and its conjugate base: a buffer. B + C: mixing acetic acid with hydrochloric acid is just a mixture of two acids. HCl ionises completely, and there is no significant acetate (conjugate base) present, since the extra $H^+$ suppresses acetic acid's ionisation, so there is no base to react with added acid and no buffer.

questions.question: Acetic acid, $CH_3COOH$, can exist as a dimer, $(CH_3COOH)_2$, in the gas phase. The dimer decomposes to produce gaseous acetic acid: $(CH_3COOH)_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2CH_3COOH(g)$, $K_{eq}=3.2\times10^{-4}$ at 25 °C. The dimer is added to an empty sealed 1.0 L vessel at a concentration of $1.5\times10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$ and allowed to reach equilibrium at 25 °C. Calculate the concentration of gaseous acetic acid $CH_3COOH(g)$ in the resulting gas mixture.
questions.answer: Let $x$ be the concentration of dimer that reacts: $[(CH_3COOH)_2]=1.5\times10^{-3}-x$, $[CH_3COOH]=2x$. $$K_{eq}=\frac{[CH_3COOH]^2}{[(CH_3COOH)_2]}=\frac{4x^2}{1.5\times10^{-3}-x}=3.2\times10^{-4}.$$ The decomposition is not small (about 20%), so the simplifying approximation $1.5\times10^{-3}-x\approx1.5\times10^{-3}$ is not valid; solve the quadratic $4x^2+3.2\times10^{-4}x-4.8\times10^{-7}=0$: $x=3.1\times10^{-4}$. $$[CH_3COOH]=2x=6.2\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}.$$ (The school's sample answer used the approximation and gave $6.9\times10^{-4}$ M, which is about 11% too high.)

questions.question: Calculate the percentage of the dimer that is converted into gaseous acetic acid at room temperature (for the system in part (a), initial dimer $1.5\times10^{-3}$ M).
questions.answer: $\%$ converted $=\dfrac{x}{[(CH_3COOH)_2]_{initial}}\times100=\dfrac{3.1\times10^{-4}}{1.5\times10^{-3}}\times100=21\%$ (using the exact solution to the quadratic; the school's approximate value was 23%).

questions.question: If the pressure of the reaction system $(CH_3COOH)_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2CH_3COOH(g)$ increased, explain whether formation of the monomer or dimer would be favoured.
questions.answer: Formation of the dimer would be favoured. Increasing the pressure (by decreasing the volume) is opposed by the system shifting to the side with fewer moles of gas (Le Châtelier's principle). The reverse reaction forms 1 mol of dimer from 2 mol of monomer, compared with the forward reaction producing 2 mol of monomer from 1 mol of dimer, so the equilibrium shifts to the left, towards the dimer.

questions.question: The alcohol shown below is heated with acidified permanganate ($MnO_4^-/H^+$). What is the systematic name for the product of the reaction?
questions.answer: The reactant is 3-methylbutan-1-ol, a primary alcohol, which is oxidised by acidified permanganate to a carboxylic acid with the same carbon chain: 3-methylbutanoic acid (D).

questions.question: Cinnamic acid is an organic substance that partly contributes to the flavour of oil of cinnamon. A structure of cinnamic acid is shown. Which of the following reagents would you expect to react with cinnamic acid under the conditions given?
questions.answer: Cinnamic acid contains a $C=C$ double bond and a carboxyl group. The $C=C$ allows addition polymerisation (copolymerisation with ethene) and addition of $Br_2$ (decolourising bromine water) at room temperature. The $-COOH$ group reacts with methanol, with sulfuric acid catalyst, in esterification to form methyl cinnamate. All three reactions occur (A).
options: $CH_2CH_2$ and catalyst: Yes; $Br_2(aq)$ at room temperature: Yes; $CH_3OH$ and $H_2SO_4$ catalyst: Yes
$CH_2CH_2$ and catalyst: Yes; $Br_2(aq)$ at room temperature: No; $CH_3OH$ and $H_2SO_4$ catalyst: Yes
$CH_2CH_2$ and catalyst: No; $Br_2(aq)$ at room temperature: Yes; $CH_3OH$ and $H_2SO_4$ catalyst: Yes
$CH_2CH_2$ and catalyst: No; $Br_2(aq)$ at room temperature: Yes; $CH_3OH$ and $H_2SO_4$ catalyst: No

questions.question: The general formula of a triglyceride is shown. Which one of the following equations represents the hydrolysis of a triglyceride?
questions.answer: Hydrolysis of a triglyceride is the reaction with three molecules of water: water adds across each ester linkage to form glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol, with three $-OH$ groups) and three carboxylic acid ($RCOOH$) molecules (A).

questions.question: A liquid mixture of 50% ethanol and 50% water was distilled in the apparatus shown. The boiling point of ethanol is $78^\circ$C and that of water is $100^\circ$C. As the mixture was heated, the temperature shown by the thermometer initially rose but then remained constant at $78^\circ$C for some time. Which one of the following statements about the percentage of ethanol in the vapours at points $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ (up the fractionating column), when the temperature is at a constant $78^\circ$C, is true?
questions.answer: The column is cooler higher up. As the vapour rises, the less volatile component (water) condenses and runs back down, while the more volatile ethanol continues up. The proportion of ethanol in the vapour therefore increases from $X$ to $Y$ to $Z$ (B).
options: The percentage of ethanol in the vapours at $X$ is equal to 50%.
The percentages of ethanol in the vapours increase in order at positions $X$, $Y$ and $Z$.
The percentages of ethanol in the vapours at $Y$ and $Z$ are equal but greater than at $X$.
The percentages of ethanol in the vapours at $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are equal but greater than 50%.

questions.question: The diagram shows the structural formula of prop-1-ene. How many signals would it show in $^{13}$C NMR and proton ($^1$H) NMR?
questions.answer: There are three carbon environments ($CH_3$, $=CH-$ and $=CH_2$), so three $^{13}C$ signals. In the proton spectrum the $CH_3$ hydrogens give one signal and the $=CH-$ hydrogen gives another. The two hydrogens on the $=CH_2$ carbon are not equivalent (one is cis and one trans to the methyl group, because rotation about the double bond is restricted), so they give two separate signals. Total: 4 proton signals and 3 carbon signals (D).

questions.question: Nitrogen dioxide (a brown gas) and dinitrogen tetroxide (a colourless gas) are both oxides of nitrogen. They are in equilibrium according to the equation $2NO_2(g)\rightleftharpoons N_2O_4(g)$. An equilibrium mixture of the two gases at room temperature is light brown but at higher temperatures the colour becomes a much deeper brown. What conclusion can be drawn from this observation?
questions.answer: Raising the temperature produces more brown $NO_2$, so the equilibrium shifts to the left. By Le Chatelier's principle, the system opposes the temperature rise by absorbing heat, so the reverse reaction is endothermic (and the forward reaction is exothermic) (A).
options: The reverse reaction in the equation is endothermic.
The forward reaction in the equation is endothermic.
The brown colour is due to the strong nitrogen–oxygen bonds in $NO_2$.
The equilibrium concentration of $N_2O_4$ is not dependent on temperature.

questions.question: Hydrogen gas reacts with iodine gas to form hydrogen iodide according to the equation $H_2(g)+I_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2HI(g)$ at 700 K. At equilibrium, the concentrations of $H_2$, $I_2$ and $HI$ are $0.214$, $0.214$ and $1.57$ mol L$^{-1}$ respectively. What is the value of the equilibrium constant for this reaction?
What will happen when sulfuric acid is added to a saturated solution of the sparingly soluble calcium sulfate? ($K_{sp}(CaSO_4)=2.4\times10^{-5}$)
questions.answer: In the saturated solution $CaSO_4(s)\rightleftharpoons Ca^{2+}(aq)+SO_4^{2-}(aq)$ and $K_{sp}=[Ca^{2+}][SO_4^{2-}]$. Sulfuric acid adds $SO_4^{2-}$ (common ion), so the ionic product exceeds $K_{sp}$ and the equilibrium shifts to the left (Le Chatelier), precipitating $CaSO_4$. The ion concentrations then decrease over time until $[Ca^{2+}][SO_4^{2-}]=K_{sp}$ again. The $H^+$ ions have no effect (D).
options: The concentration of calcium and sulfate ions will increase over time due to the presence of $H^+$ ions.
The concentration of calcium and sulfate ions will decrease over time due to the presence of $H^+$ ions.
The concentration of calcium and sulfate ions will increase over time due to the presence of $SO_4^{2-}$ ions.
The concentration of calcium and sulfate ions will decrease over time due to the presence of $SO_4^{2-}$ ions.

questions.question: At a certain temperature, $K_{eq}$ for the reaction $2O_3(g)\rightleftharpoons3O_2(g)$ is 75. $0.3$ mol of $O_3$ and $1.5$ mol of $O_2$ were introduced into a 5 L reaction vessel. Which row correctly identifies the direction of the equilibrium shift and the reason for the shift?
questions.answer: $[O_3]=\frac{0.3}{5}=0.06$ M and $[O_2]=\frac{1.5}{5}=0.30$ M. $Q=\dfrac{[O_2]^3}{[O_3]^2}=\dfrac{(0.30)^3}{(0.06)^2}=7.5$. Since $Q<K_{eq}=75$, the system must shift to the right (towards products) to reach equilibrium (D).

questions.question: Hydrogen is produced on an industrial scale from methane by the reaction $2H_2O(g)+CH_4(g)\rightleftharpoons CO_2(g)+4H_2(g)$. If an inert gas is added to the equilibrium system at constant temperature and constant volume, the concentration of $H_2$ will
questions.answer: Adding an inert gas at constant volume does not change the concentration (or partial pressure) of any reacting species, so $Q$ is unchanged and still equals $K$. The equilibrium is not disturbed and $[H_2]$ does not change (C).

questions.question: The sulfate ($SO_4^{2-}$) content of a plant fertiliser is to be determined by gravimetric analysis of a 2.5 g sample of fertiliser. The first part of this analysis would involve
questions.answer: The sulfate in the solid fertiliser must first be brought into solution (dissolved in water, with any insoluble material then filtered off) so that all the $SO_4^{2-}$ is available to react with the precipitating reagent (C).
options: filtering the sulfate ions from the insoluble material in the fertiliser
dissolving the sulfate from the fertiliser into water
adding an indicator to an aliquot of the sulfate solution

questions.question: In the gravimetric analysis of the sulfate in a fertiliser, an excess solution is added to produce a precipitate. This solution is known as the precipitating reagent. Which precipitating reagent would be the most suitable for this analysis?
questions.answer: Barium ions form the insoluble precipitate $BaSO_4$ with sulfate: $Ba^{2+}(aq)+SO_4^{2-}(aq)\to BaSO_4(s)$. $Na^+$, $K^+$ and $Cu^{2+}$ sulfates are all soluble, and $CuSO_4$ would add sulfate rather than precipitate it (B).

questions.question: In the gravimetric analysis of the sulfate in a fertiliser, which of the following errors in experimental procedure would produce a percentage of sulfate in the fertiliser that is LESS than the true value?
questions.answer: If excess precipitating reagent is not added, not all of the sulfate precipitates, so the mass of precipitate is too low and the calculated percentage of sulfate is too low (C). Not washing the precipitate leaves soluble impurities, and not drying it fully leaves water, so in both cases the measured mass is too high.
options: Failure to wash the precipitate with distilled water.
Failure to dry the precipitate to a constant mass.
Failure to add an excess amount of precipitating reagent.
Failure to let the precipitate dry in an oven.

questions.question: A 20 mL aliquot of vinegar is titrated with $15$ mL of $0.10$ M NaOH. The vinegar is in the conical flask ($B$) and the NaOH is in the burette ($A$). The piece of equipment labelled $A$ should be
questions.answer: $A$ is the burette, which contains the titrant. It should be rinsed with the solution it is to deliver ($0.10$ M NaOH) so that residual water does not dilute the titrant, and then filled with that solution (C).
options: rinsed with distilled water and filled with 20 mL of vinegar
rinsed with distilled water and filled with 0.10 M NaOH.
rinsed with 0.10 M NaOH and filled with 0.10 M NaOH
rinsed with vinegar and filled with 20 mL of vinegar

questions.question: A 20 mL aliquot of vinegar (in the conical flask, $B$) is titrated with $0.10$ M NaOH from the burette ($A$); the titre is $15$ mL when the equipment is prepared correctly. If the equipment labelled $A$ (the burette) is rinsed with distilled water only before the titration,
questions.answer: The water left in the burette dilutes the NaOH, so the concentration of the titrant is lower than $0.10$ M. A larger volume of the diluted NaOH is therefore needed to neutralise the same amount of acetic acid, so the titre is greater than 15 mL (C).
options: the volume of NaOH used will be 15 mL
the volume of vinegar used will be less than 15 mL
the volume of NaOH used will be greater than 15 mL
the volume of NaOH used will be exactly 20 mL

questions.question: A 20 mL aliquot of vinegar is pipetted into a conical flask ($B$) and titrated with $0.10$ M NaOH from the burette; the titre is $15$ mL when the equipment is prepared correctly. If the equipment labelled $B$ (the conical flask) is rinsed with distilled water before the titration,
questions.answer: Water in the conical flask does not change the number of moles of acid that were pipetted into it, so the volume of NaOH needed to neutralise it is unchanged (A).
options: the volume of NaOH used will be 15 mL
the volume of vinegar used will be less than 15 mL
the volume of NaOH used will be greater than 15 mL
the volume of NaOH used will be exactly 20 mL

questions.question: Which of the following rows correctly corresponds with the symbols that describe the thermodynamic properties of a system?
questions.answer: $\Delta G$ is the change in Gibbs free energy, $\Delta H$ is the change in heat content (enthalpy) and $\Delta S$ is the change in randomness (entropy) (A).
options: $\Delta G$: change in Gibbs free energy; $\Delta H$: change in heat content; $\Delta S$: change in randomness
$\Delta G$: total Gibbs free energy; $\Delta H$: total heat content; $\Delta S$: total randomness
$\Delta G$: initial Gibbs free energy; $\Delta H$: initial heat content; $\Delta S$: initial randomness
$\Delta G$: change in randomness; $\Delta H$: change in Gibbs free energy; $\Delta S$: change in heat content

questions.question: For a chemical equilibrium $A+B\rightleftharpoons2C$, the value of the equilibrium constant ($K_{eq}$) is $4.2\times10^{-5}$. What is the value of the equilibrium constant for the reverse reaction?
questions.answer: The equilibrium constant for the reverse reaction is the reciprocal: $K_{rev}=\dfrac{1}{4.2\times10^{-5}}=2.38\times10^{4}$ (C).

questions.question: When an ionic solid dissolves in water and forms a saturated solution, the process can be described in stages. These stages include: I. When two opposing rates are equal, the system reaches equilibrium. II. Aqueous ions arrive at the solid lattice and become part of it. III. The ionic lattice dissociates into individual ions. IV. The ionic lattice is surrounded by water molecules. Which of the following gives the correct order of stages?
questions.answer:
Dissolving begins when the lattice is surrounded by water molecules (IV), and the system ends when the opposing rates of dissolving and re-crystallising are equal and equilibrium is reached (I). Dissociation of the lattice (III) and ions returning to the lattice (II) occur in between, once dissolving has begun and as equilibrium is approached. Only C begins with IV and ends with I (C).

Note: strictly, the chemical order is IV, III, II, I; none of the options gives that order, but C is the only one starting with IV and ending with I.

questions.question: The diagram shows a portion of a polymer. Which of the structures represents the monomer?
questions.answer: The polymer is an addition polymer with a $-CH_2-CH(COOH)-$ repeating unit. Its monomer is an alkene with a carboxylic acid group, $CH_2=CH-COOH$ (propenoic/acrylic acid), which is structure D. The other structures have the wrong number of bonds on one or more atoms or the wrong connectivity.

questions.question: Carbon monoxide, $CO$, reacts with ammonia, $NH_3$, to produce highly toxic hydrogen cyanide, $HCN$, as well as carbon dioxide and hydrogen. The reaction is endothermic: $2CO(g)+NH_3(g)\rightleftharpoons HCN(g)+CO_2(g)+H_2(g)$. Write the expression for the equilibrium constant for this reaction.

Carbon monoxide reacts with ammonia: $2CO(g)+NH_3(g)\rightleftharpoons HCN(g)+CO_2(g)+H_2(g)$. In one experiment, a mixture of $CO$ and $NH_3$, together with a suitable catalyst, was injected into a sealed 100 mL gas syringe and allowed to come to equilibrium. The equilibrium mixture contained $[CO]=0.0025$ M, $[NH_3]=0.00125$ M and $[HCN]=0.0042$ M. (The $HCN$, $CO_2$ and $H_2$ were formed only from this reaction, in a 1:1:1 ratio.) Calculate the equilibrium constant for the reaction at this temperature.

prev.question: Carbon monoxide, $CO$, reacts with ammonia, $NH_3$, to produce highly toxic hydrogen cyanide, $HCN$, as well as carbon dioxide and hydrogen. The reaction is endothermic: $2CO(g)+NH_3(g)\rightleftharpoons HCN(g)+CO_2(g)+H_2(g)$. Write the expression for the equilibrium constant for this reaction.

questions.question: Analysts investigated the effect of two different changes on the equilibrium system $2CO(g)+NH_3(g)\rightleftharpoons HCN(g)+CO_2(g)+H_2(g)$ (endothermic) by monitoring the amount of $HCN$ (in moles) present in the gas mixture. State whether the amount of $HCN$ will increase, decrease or have no effect for each change: (1) halving the volume of the gas mixture, keeping the temperature constant; (2) returning the volume of the gas mixture to 100 mL and then injecting some powdered palladium into the gas syringe (palladium absorbs $H_2$ gas onto its surface).
questions.answer: (1) No effect. There are 3 mol of gas on each side of the equation, so changing the volume (pressure) does not favour either direction. (2) Increase. Palladium removes $H_2$, a product, so the equilibrium shifts to the right to replace it, producing more $HCN$.

questions.question: At equilibrium in a 100 mL gas syringe the concentrations are $[HCN]=0.0042$ M and $[NH_3]=0.00125$ M for the system $2CO(g)+NH_3(g)\rightleftharpoons HCN(g)+CO_2(g)+H_2(g)$. Complete the concentration–time graph on the axes provided to show what will happen to the concentrations of $HCN$ and $NH_3$ in the equilibrium mixture when the volume of the gas mixture is suddenly halved at constant temperature.
questions.answer:
Halving the volume instantly doubles every concentration: $[HCN]$ rises from $0.0042$ M to $0.0084$ M and $[NH_3]$ from $0.00125$ M to $0.0025$ M. There are equal numbers of moles of gas on each side, so there is no shift in equilibrium afterwards and both concentrations stay constant at these new values.

Note: the marking guide gives the final $[NH_3]$ as 0.0026 M; doubling 0.00125 M gives 0.0025 M.

prev.question: Analysts investigated the effect of two different changes on the equilibrium system $2CO(g)+NH_3(g)\rightleftharpoons HCN(g)+CO_2(g)+H_2(g)$ (endothermic) by monitoring the amount of $HCN$ (in moles) present in the gas mixture. State whether the amount of $HCN$ will increase, decrease or have no effect for each change: (1) halving the volume of the gas mixture, keeping the temperature constant; (2) returning the volume of the gas mixture to 100 mL and then injecting some powdered palladium into the gas syringe (palladium absorbs $H_2$ gas onto its surface).
prev.answer: (1) No effect. There are 3 mol of gas on each side of the equation, so changing the volume (pressure) does not favour either direction. (2) Increase. Palladium removes $H_2$, a product, so the equilibrium shifts to the right to replace it, producing more $HCN$.

questions.question: $CO$ gas is produced when a hydrocarbon fuel, such as butane, $C_4H_{10}$, is burnt in a limited air supply. Write the balanced equation for the combustion of $C_4H_{10}$ in a limited air supply, assuming that $CO$ is the only carbon-based oxidation product.

Haemoglobin in red blood cells takes up $O_2$ from the air in an equilibrium reaction (Equation 1): $Hb_4(aq)+4O_2(aq)\rightleftharpoons Hb_4O_8(aq)$, with equilibrium constant $K_1$. $CO$ molecules can also attach to haemoglobin (Equation 2): $Hb_4(aq)+4CO(aq)\rightleftharpoons Hb_4(CO)_4(aq)$, with equilibrium constant $K_2$. If the concentration of $CO$ in the air inside a burning building increases to 800 ppm, anyone exposed to it will quickly lose consciousness, even if oxygen is present. To revive them, they must be given pure oxygen. What conclusions can be made about the relative values of the equilibrium constants $K_1$ and $K_2$?
questions.answer: $K_2$ is much larger than $K_1$ ($K_2\gg K_1$). $CO$ and $O_2$ compete for the haemoglobin, and even at a very low concentration of $CO$ (800 ppm, compared with about 21% $O_2$ in air) the $CO$ binds in preference to $O_2$ and the haemoglobin–$CO$ complex dominates. For this to happen, the position of equilibrium of Equation 2 must lie much further to the right than that of Equation 1, which means a much greater equilibrium constant. (Giving pure $O_2$ raises $[O_2]$ enough to shift Equation 1 to the right and displace the $CO$.)

questions.question: Claire is analysing a sample of paint to determine the organic solvents that are present. She separates the compounds and analyses each using infra-red (IR) spectroscopy and $^{13}$C and $^1$H NMR spectroscopy. One compound has the molecular formula $C_5H_{10}O$. The IR spectrum of this compound is shown. From the IR spectrum, identify the organic family to which this compound belongs. Justify your answer by referring to the relevant wave number.
questions.answer: The compound is a ketone or an aldehyde. The strong, sharp absorption at about $1700$ cm$^{-1}$ corresponds to a $C=O$ (carbonyl) group (aldehydes $1660$–$1745$ cm$^{-1}$, ketones $1680$–$1850$ cm$^{-1}$). There is no broad $O-H$ absorption at $3230$–$3550$ cm$^{-1}$ (or $2500$–$3000$ cm$^{-1}$), so it is not an alcohol or a carboxylic acid. With only one oxygen atom in $C_5H_{10}O$ it cannot be an ester or carboxylic acid. The peak near $3000$ cm$^{-1}$ is the $C-H$ stretch, present in all organic families.

questions.question: Claire isolates a compound with the molecular formula $C_5H_{10}O$ from a sample of paint. Its IR spectrum shows a strong absorption at about $1700$ cm$^{-1}$ (a carbonyl group) and no $O-H$ absorption. Its $^{13}$C NMR spectrum has peaks at about $215$, $35$ and $9$ ppm. Its $^1$H NMR spectrum has two peaks: at $1.0$ ppm (splitting pattern: 3, i.e. a triplet) and $2.4$ ppm (splitting pattern: 4, i.e. a quartet). The spectra are shown. Draw a structural formula for this compound that is consistent with the data provided, and explain your reasoning by referring to the data.
questions.answer: The compound is pentan-3-one, $CH_3CH_2COCH_2CH_3$. **Symmetry:** $C_5H_{10}O$ has five carbons but the $^{13}C$ spectrum shows only three peaks, so some carbons are in the same environment, and the $^1H$ spectrum has only two peaks, so there are only two hydrogen environments. This indicates a symmetrical molecule. **$^{13}C$ NMR:** the peak at $215$ ppm is a carbonyl carbon in a ketone ($R_2C=O$, $205$–$220$ ppm); $35$ ppm is a $R-CH_2-R$ carbon ($20$–$45$ ppm); $9$ ppm is a $R-CH_3$ carbon ($8$–$25$ ppm). **$^1H$ NMR:** the $1.0$ ppm peak is a $R-CH_3$ ($0.9$–$1.0$ ppm), split into a triplet by the two hydrogens on the adjacent $CH_2$; the $2.4$ ppm peak is $-CH_2-$ next to the carbonyl ($R-CO-CH_2-$, $2.1$–$2.7$ ppm), split into a quartet by the three hydrogens of the adjacent $CH_3$. This fits $CH_3CH_2-CO-CH_2CH_3$ only; an aldehyde would give more than three carbon environments.

questions.question: Using IUPAC nomenclature, name the three compounds shown (Compound 1, Compound 2 and Compound 3).
questions.answer: Compound 1: propan-1-amine ($CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2$). Compound 2: 2,2-dimethylpropane ($C(CH_3)_4$). Compound 3: propanamide ($CH_3CH_2CONH_2$).

questions.question: Compound 1 is propan-1-amine ($CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2$), Compound 2 is 2,2-dimethylpropane ($C(CH_3)_4$) and Compound 3 is propanamide ($CH_3CH_2CONH_2$). Compare the intermolecular forces in these three molecules and predict the order of boiling points (lowest to highest) of these molecules. Explain your predictions.
questions.answer: Order of increasing boiling point: Compound 2 < Compound 1 < Compound 3. The stronger the intermolecular forces, the more energy needed to separate the molecules, so the higher the boiling point. Compound 2 is a non-polar alkane with only weak dispersion forces. Compound 1 is a primary amine: the polar $N-H$ bonds allow hydrogen bonding between molecules (stronger than dispersion forces) as well as dispersion forces. Compound 3 is an amide with a very polar $-CONH_2$ group: the $N-H$ hydrogens bond to the $C=O$ oxygen of neighbouring molecules, and the planar group allows two hydrogen bonds between a pair of molecules (forming dimers or a network), so it has the strongest intermolecular forces and the highest boiling point.

questions.question: Compound 3 is propanamide, $CH_3CH_2CONH_2$. Identify how compound 3 could be produced by a chemical reaction. Include an equation in your response.
questions.answer: React propanoic acid with ammonia and heat the mixture (the ammonium propanoate salt formed dehydrates): $CH_3CH_2COOH+NH_3\to CH_3CH_2CONH_2+H_2O$.

questions.question: The table shows acid dissociation constants at $25^\circ$C. Identify the weakest acid in the table and determine the $pK_a$ value for this acid.
questions.answer:
The weakest acid has the smallest $K_a$: water, $H_2O$ ($K_a=1.0\times10^{-14}$). $pK_a=-\log_{10}(1.0\times10^{-14})=14.00$.

Note: the table's value for water is used; the data-sheet value of $K_a$ for water is $K_w$.

questions.question: Hydrocyanic acid ($HCN$) has $K_a=6.2\times10^{-10}$ at $25^\circ$C. Calculate the pH of a $0.10$ M solution of hydrocyanic acid.
questions.answer: $HCN(aq)+H_2O(l)\rightleftharpoons CN^-(aq)+H_3O^+(aq)$, $K_a=\dfrac{[CN^-][H_3O^+]}{[HCN]}=6.2\times10^{-10}$. Let $[H_3O^+]=x$, then $[CN^-]=x$ and $[HCN]=0.10-x\approx0.10$ (since $x$ is very small). $x^2=(6.2\times10^{-10})(0.10)=6.2\times10^{-11}$, so $[H_3O^+]=7.87\times10^{-6}$ M and $pH=-\log_{10}(7.87\times10^{-6})=5.10$.

questions.question: A buffer solution is prepared by combining $100$ mL of $0.10$ M $HCN$ and $100$ mL of $0.10$ M $NaCN$. Given $K_a(HCN)=6.2\times10^{-10}$, calculate the pH of this buffer solution and explain the classification of the solution as a buffer.
questions.answer: On mixing, the volume doubles, so $[HCN]=[CN^-]=0.050$ M. $K_a=\dfrac{[CN^-][H_3O^+]}{[HCN]}$ gives $[H_3O^+]=K_a\dfrac{[HCN]}{[CN^-]}=6.2\times10^{-10}\times\dfrac{0.050}{0.050}=6.2\times10^{-10}$ M, so $pH=9.21$. The solution is a buffer because it contains a weak acid ($HCN$) and its conjugate base ($CN^-$) in comparable concentrations, so it resists changes in pH when small amounts of strong acid or base are added. Added $H^+$ is consumed by $CN^-$ ($CN^-+H^+\to HCN$) and added $OH^-$ is consumed by $HCN$ ($HCN+OH^-\to CN^-+H_2O$). The ratio $[HCN]/[CN^-]$ changes only slightly, so the pH stays close to $9.21$.

questions.question: A solution contains four cations: $Ag^+$, $Ba^{2+}$, $Ca^{2+}$ and $Fe^{2+}$. The flow chart represents the steps taken to identify each cation: the mixture is treated with excess $HCl$ and filtered (precipitate 1, filtrate 1); filtrate 1 is treated with excess $NH_3$ and filtered (precipitate 2, filtrate 2); filtrate 2 is treated with $H_2SO_4$ and filtered (precipitate 3, filtrate 3). Name precipitates 1, 2 and 3 and write the ionic equation for the formation of each precipitate. Suggest a test to confirm the identity of the remaining cation in filtrate 3.
questions.answer:
Precipitate 1 is silver chloride, $AgCl$: $Ag^+(aq)+Cl^-(aq)\to AgCl(s)$. Precipitate 2 is iron(II) hydroxide, $Fe(OH)_2$: $Fe^{2+}(aq)+2OH^-(aq)\to Fe(OH)_2(s)$ (the $OH^-$ comes from the ammonia solution). Precipitate 3 is barium sulfate, $BaSO_4$: $Ba^{2+}(aq)+SO_4^{2-}(aq)\to BaSO_4(s)$. The remaining cation in filtrate 3 is $Ca^{2+}$. Test: a flame test, giving an orange-red flame (or add $NaOH$ solution, which gives a white precipitate of $Ca(OH)_2$ that does not dissolve in excess).

Note: the marking guide's equations for precipitates 2 and 3 were unbalanced or had the wrong charge ($Fe^{2+}+OH^-$ and $SO_4^{2+}$); the balanced equations are given above.

questions.question: Different tests are used to distinguish between primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols. Describe ONE test for each type of alcohol and include the chemical reaction.
questions.answer:
Heat the alcohol with an oxidising agent such as acidified potassium permanganate ($KMnO_4/H^+$, purple to colourless) or acidified potassium dichromate (orange to green). **Primary alcohol** (e.g. ethanol): the oxidant is decolourised as the alcohol is oxidised, via the aldehyde, to a carboxylic acid: $CH_3CH_2OH+2[O]\to CH_3COOH+H_2O$. The acid can be confirmed by adding a carbonate: effervescence of $CO_2$ gas, $2CH_3COOH+Na_2CO_3\to2CH_3COONa+CO_2+H_2O$. **Secondary alcohol** (e.g. propan-2-ol): the oxidant is also decolourised, forming a ketone: $CH_3CH(OH)CH_3+[O]\to CH_3COCH_3+H_2O$. No gas is produced when a carbonate is added (no acid). **Tertiary alcohol**: no reaction with the oxidising agent, so the solution remains purple (or orange).

Note: the marking guide's carbonate equation was not balanced; the balanced equation is shown.

questions.question: The $K_{sp}$ value for magnesium hydroxide is $5.61\times10^{-12}$. Write the equation for the solubility equilibrium for magnesium hydroxide.
questions.answer: $Mg(OH)_2(s)\rightleftharpoons Mg^{2+}(aq)+2OH^-(aq)$

questions.question: Write the $K_{sp}$ expression for magnesium hydroxide, $Mg(OH)_2$.
The $K_{sp}$ value for magnesium hydroxide is $5.61\times10^{-12}$ at $25^\circ$C. Calculate the solubility of magnesium hydroxide at $25^\circ$C.
questions.answer: Let the solubility be $x$ mol L$^{-1}$. $Mg(OH)_2(s)\rightleftharpoons Mg^{2+}(aq)+2OH^-(aq)$ gives $[Mg^{2+}]=x$ and $[OH^-]=2x$. $K_{sp}=x(2x)^2=4x^3=5.61\times10^{-12}$, so $x^3=1.4025\times10^{-12}$ and $x=1.12\times10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$. (So $[OH^-]=2.24\times10^{-4}$ M.)

questions.question:
A green leaf with a mass of $0.320$ g is analysed for its chlorophyll content by UV–visible spectroscopy. The chlorophyll is extracted and dissolved in $250$ mL of solvent. A sample of the solution is placed in a UV–visible spectrometer with the wavelength set at $410$ nm. The absorbance of the chlorophyll solution at this wavelength is $0.21$. The absorbance values of four standard chlorophyll solutions are:

| Concentration (M) | Absorbance |
|---|---|
| $2.5\\times10^{-4}$ | $0.120$ |
| $5.0\\times10^{-4}$ | $0.239$ |
| $7.5\\times10^{-4}$ | $0.351$ |
| $1.0\\times10^{-3}$ | $0.483$ |

Using the grid provided, construct a calibration graph showing the absorbance of the chlorophyll standards.
questions.answer: Plot absorbance (vertical axis, 0 to 0.60) against concentration in M (horizontal axis, 0 to 0.0012) with a suitable scale, mark the four points accurately and draw a straight line of best fit through them (it passes very close to the origin). The graph shows a linear relationship, as expected from the Beer–Lambert law.

questions.question: A calibration line for chlorophyll at $410$ nm is a straight line through the points ($2.5\times10^{-4}$ M, $0.120$), ($5.0\times10^{-4}$ M, $0.239$), ($7.5\times10^{-4}$ M, $0.351$) and ($1.0\times10^{-3}$ M, $0.483$). The chlorophyll solution extracted from a leaf (250 mL) has an absorbance of $0.21$ at this wavelength. What is the concentration of chlorophyll in g L$^{-1}$ in the 250 mL solution? $M_r$(chlorophyll) $=893.5$ g mol$^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
From the line of best fit (gradient about $480$ M$^{-1}$), an absorbance of $0.21$ corresponds to $c\approx4.4\times10^{-4}$ M. Concentration in g L$^{-1}$ $=4.4\times10^{-4}\times893.5=0.39$ g L$^{-1}$.

Note: readings from the graph of $4.2$–$4.4\times10^{-4}$ M are acceptable; the marking guide read $4.2\times10^{-4}$ M, giving $0.375$ g L$^{-1}$ (its working line also printed $0.384$ g L$^{-1}$, an arithmetic slip).

questions.question: The chlorophyll from a $0.320$ g green leaf was dissolved in $250$ mL of solvent, giving a concentration of $0.39$ g L$^{-1}$ (determined by UV–visible spectroscopy). What is the percentage by mass of chlorophyll in the leaf?
questions.answer:
Mass of chlorophyll $=0.39\ \text{g L}^{-1}\times0.250\ \text{L}=0.0985$ g (about $0.098$ g). Percentage by mass $=\dfrac{0.0985}{0.320}\times100=31\%$ (about 30.8%).

Note: using the marking guide's $0.375$ g L$^{-1}$ gives $0.0938$ g and $29.3\%$, which is also acceptable.

questions.question: Why was light with a wavelength of $410$ nm chosen for the UV–visible analysis of chlorophyll?
questions.answer: Chlorophyll absorbs strongly at about $410$ nm (violet/blue light), so this wavelength gives the highest absorbance (greatest sensitivity) for a measurable change with concentration.

questions.question: A solution of hydrochloric acid was standardised by titration against sodium carbonate solution. All glassware was rinsed correctly to remove possible contamination; hydrochloric acid was placed in the burette and $25.0$ mL of sodium carbonate solution was pipetted into the conical flask. Identify the chemical used to rinse the pipette and justify your answer.
questions.answer: The pipette should be rinsed with the sodium carbonate solution. Rinsing with water would dilute the solution that is drawn into the pipette, changing the number of moles of sodium carbonate delivered and making the standardisation inaccurate. Rinsing with the sodium carbonate solution ensures that any residue in the pipette has the same concentration.

questions.question: A solution of hydrochloric acid was standardised by titration against sodium carbonate solution. Explain why sodium carbonate solution, rather than sodium hydroxide solution, is used to standardise the hydrochloric acid.
questions.answer: Standardisation requires a primary standard: a substance that can be obtained pure, is stable, does not absorb water or react with $CO_2$ in the air, can be weighed accurately and has a relatively high molar mass (to minimise weighing error). Sodium carbonate meets these requirements ($M=106$ g mol$^{-1}$). Sodium hydroxide absorbs water and reacts with atmospheric $CO_2$, is not available as a pure stable solid, and has a lower molar mass ($40$ g mol$^{-1}$), so a solution of exactly known concentration cannot be made by weighing it.

questions.question: Seashells contain a mixture of carbonate compounds. Standard hydrochloric acid ($0.200$ mol L$^{-1}$) was used to determine the percentage by mass of carbonate ions in a seashell. A $0.154$ g sample of the seashell was placed in a conical flask and $50.0$ mL of the standardised hydrochloric acid was added. At the completion of the reaction, the mixture in the flask was titrated with $0.250$ mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide, and $29.5$ mL of sodium hydroxide was used. Calculate the percentage by mass of carbonate ions in the sample of the seashell.
questions.answer:
$CO_3^{2-}+2HCl\to2Cl^-+CO_2+H_2O$. $n(HCl)_{added}=0.200\times0.0500=0.0100$ mol. $n(NaOH)=0.250\times0.0295=0.007375$ mol $=n(HCl)_{excess}$. $n(HCl)_{reacted}=0.0100-0.007375=0.002625$ mol. $n(CO_3^{2-})=\frac12\times0.002625=0.0013125$ mol. $m(CO_3^{2-})=0.0013125\times60.01=0.0788$ g. Percentage $=\dfrac{0.0788}{0.154}\times100=51.1\%$.

Note: the marking guide gives 51.2% (rounding the mass first); answers of 51.1–51.2% were accepted.

questions.question: A student was researching calcium sulfate ($CaSO_4$) and calcium carbonate ($CaCO_3$). Their first step was to look at the solubility constants ($K_{sp}$) for the two compounds: $K_{sp}(CaSO_4)=4.93\times10^{-5}$ and $K_{sp}(CaCO_3)\approx3.4\times10^{-9}$ at $25^\circ$C. Discuss the solubilities of these two compounds at $25^\circ$C.
questions.answer: Both compounds are sparingly soluble (small $K_{sp}$ values). For each, $K_{sp}=[Ca^{2+}][anion]$, and because they have the same 1:1 stoichiometry, the $K_{sp}$ values can be compared directly. $CaSO_4$ has the much larger $K_{sp}$ ($4.93\times10^{-5}$ compared with $\sim3.4\times10^{-9}$), so it is considerably more soluble than $CaCO_3$.

questions.question: Derive the equilibrium expression for calcium sulfate and use this to calculate the solubility (in mol L$^{-1}$) of calcium sulfate. $K_{sp}(CaSO_4)=4.93\times10^{-5}$. Show your working.
questions.answer: $CaSO_4(s)\rightleftharpoons Ca^{2+}(aq)+SO_4^{2-}(aq)$, so $K_{sp}=[Ca^{2+}][SO_4^{2-}]$. If the solubility is $s$ then $[Ca^{2+}]=[SO_4^{2-}]=s$, so $s^2=4.93\times10^{-5}$ and $s=\sqrt{4.93\times10^{-5}}=7.02\times10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

questions.question: Outline ONE practice of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples that uses solubility equilibria.
questions.answer: Some Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander groups in northern Australia use cycad seeds as a food source. The seeds contain toxins that make them poisonous if eaten untreated. The toxins are much more soluble in water than the nutrients in the seeds, so prolonged soaking or leaching of the seeds in (running) water removes the toxins by dissolving them, leaving the less soluble nutrients behind.

questions.question: $20$ mL of $0.010$ mol L$^{-1}$ calcium nitrate is added to $20$ mL of $0.010$ mol L$^{-1}$ sodium sulfate. Determine whether precipitation of calcium sulfate will occur. ($K_{sp}(CaSO_4)=4.93\times10^{-5}$)
questions.answer: $n(Ca^{2+})=0.010\times0.020=2.0\times10^{-4}$ mol and $n(SO_4^{2-})=0.010\times0.020=2.0\times10^{-4}$ mol. The total volume is $40$ mL $=0.040$ L, so $[Ca^{2+}]=[SO_4^{2-}]=\dfrac{2.0\times10^{-4}}{0.040}=5.0\times10^{-3}$ M. Ionic product $=[Ca^{2+}][SO_4^{2-}]=(5.0\times10^{-3})^2=2.5\times10^{-5}$. Since $2.5\times10^{-5}<K_{sp}=4.93\times10^{-5}$, the solution is unsaturated and no precipitate will form.

questions.question: Label each of the detergents shown as anionic, cationic or non-ionic: (i) cetyltrimethylammonium bromide, (ii) the sodium salt of a steroid-based carboxylic acid (a bile salt), (iii) sodium alkylbenzenesulfonate.
questions.answer:
(i) Cationic: the hydrophilic head is a positively charged quaternary ammonium ion. (ii) Anionic: the hydrophilic head is a negatively charged carboxylate group ($-COO^-Na^+$). (iii) Anionic: the head is a negatively charged sulfonate group ($-SO_3^-Na^+$).

Note: the marking guide labelled (ii) non-ionic, but the structure is a sodium carboxylate, so it is anionic.

questions.question: Soaps can remove fats and oils from the skin because of their structure. Discuss this statement.
questions.answer: Soap is the sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain fatty acid. It has a non-polar, hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail, which is attracted to fats and oils (dispersion forces), and a negatively charged, hydrophilic carboxylate head, which is attracted to water (ion–dipole forces). When soap is rubbed on the skin with water, the tails dissolve into the oil or grease and the heads stay in the water, so the oil is surrounded by soap molecules, forming spherical micelles with the heads on the outside. The micelles are dispersed in the water and rinsed away. Soap is also a surfactant that reduces the surface tension of water, helping the water wet the skin. This dual structure is what allows soap to remove fats and oils.

questions.question: Identify the conjugate base of the hydronium ion.
questions.answer: A conjugate base is formed when an acid donates a proton. $H_3O^+\to H^++H_2O$, so the conjugate base of $H_3O^+$ is $H_2O$ (A).

questions.question: Which of the following compounds has the highest molar solubility in water at $25^\circ$C (use the $K_{sp}$ values from the data sheet)?
questions.answer: Using data sheet $K_{sp}$ values: $BaCO_3$ ($2.58\times10^{-9}$): $s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}=5\times10^{-5}$ M. $Mg_3(PO_4)_2$ ($1.04\times10^{-24}$): $K_{sp}=108s^5$, $s=6\times10^{-6}$ M. $Pb(OH)_2$ ($1.43\times10^{-20}$): $K_{sp}=4s^3$, $s=1.5\times10^{-7}$ M. $CaSO_4$ ($4.93\times10^{-5}$): $s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}=7.0\times10^{-3}$ M. $CaSO_4$ has the highest molar solubility (D).

questions.question: The graph shows how the rates of the forward and reverse reactions, as shown by the balanced equations on the graph, change over time. Which of the following statements, from the data shown, is correct?
questions.answer: The reverse rate increases from zero as products ($N_2O_4$ is not present initially; $NO_2$ builds up) accumulate, and it reaches its highest value when it becomes equal to the forward rate at equilibrium (A). The graph gives rates, not concentrations, so B cannot be deduced. The forward reaction $N_2O_4\to2NO_2$ increases the number of moles of gas, so the pressure rises (not C). At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal, non-zero rates (not D).
options: At equilibrium, the reverse reaction proceeds at its maximum rate.
After 10 s, the concentration of $NO_2(g)$ would be double that of $N_2O_4(g)$.
The pressure in the reaction vessel would decrease over the first 10 seconds.
After 10 s, any chemical reactions between the gases in the vessel have ceased.

questions.question: The graph shows the change in colour of four different indicators over a pH range of 2 to 10. An unknown solution is tested with indicator $P$, which turns purple. A fresh sample is tested with indicator $R$, which turns red. The likely pH of the unknown solution is:
questions.answer: Indicator $P$ is purple above its transition range, which ends at about pH 5.5, so the pH is above about 5.5. Indicator $R$ is red below its transition range, which starts at about pH 6.5, so the pH is below about 6.5. Only pH 6 satisfies both (B).

questions.question: Consider the compound represented by the formula $CH_3CH_2CONH_2$. What is the name of this compound?
questions.answer: The $-CONH_2$ group is an amide. With three carbons (including the carbonyl carbon) the name is propanamide (D).

questions.question: The graph shows the relationship between $\Delta H$, $T\Delta S$ and temperature in a chemical system. At $T_1$ the $\Delta G$ for the reaction is
questions.answer: $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S$. At $T_1$ ($\approx233$ K) the graph gives $\Delta H\approx-92$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ and $T\Delta S\approx-53$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, so $\Delta G\approx-92-(-53)=-39\approx-40$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ (D). (At $T_2$ the lines cross and $\Delta G=0$.)

questions.question: Methane gas was reacted with oxygen in a closed container until the following equilibrium was achieved: $2CH_4(g)+O_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2CO(g)+4H_2(g)$, $\Delta H=-76$ kJ. Which alternative correctly predicts how the quantity of hydrogen gas could be increased?
questions.answer: There are 3 mol of gas on the left and 6 mol on the right. Decreasing the pressure favours the side with more moles of gas, so the equilibrium shifts right and more $H_2$ forms (B). A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium. Raising the temperature favours the endothermic (reverse) direction for this exothermic reaction. The equilibrium constant changes only with temperature, and reducing $[CH_4]$ would shift the equilibrium left.
options: Decreasing the pressure of the system.
Increasing the temperature of the system.
Changing the equilibrium constant for the reaction by reducing the methane concentration.

questions.question: Ethanol is an alternative fuel to petrol. Consider the statements: I. Ethanol releases more energy per gram when completely combusted than petrol. II. Ethanol releases less $CO_2$ per mole of fuel combusted than petrol. III. Ethanol is less likely to undergo incomplete combustion than petrol. IV. Ethanol can be produced from non-fossil fuel resources. Which of the above statements correctly compares ethanol to petrol when used as a fuel?
questions.answer: I is false: petrol (octane and similar hydrocarbons) releases about 48 kJ g$^{-1}$ compared with about 30 kJ g$^{-1}$ for ethanol. II is true: ethanol ($C_2$) gives 2 mol $CO_2$ per mole, while petrol (about $C_8$) gives about 8. III is true: ethanol contains oxygen, so combustion is more complete. IV is true: ethanol can be made by fermentation of plant material (D).

questions.question: Cloudy ammonia is an ingredient of some household cleaners. It forms an equilibrium mixture when dissolved in water: $NH_3(aq)+H_2O(l)\rightleftharpoons NH_4^+(aq)+OH^-(aq)$. Which of the following is the equilibrium expression for the forward reaction?
questions.answer: The equilibrium expression is products over reactants, omitting the liquid water: $K=\dfrac{[NH_4^+][OH^-]}{[NH_3]}$ (A).

questions.question: Which of the following statements best explains the cleaning action of soap?
questions.answer: Soap has a charged (ionic) hydrophilic head, which interacts with polar water through ion–dipole forces, and a non-polar hydrocarbon tail, which interacts with non-polar oils and fats through dispersion forces (D).
options: The polar head group forms dispersion forces with oils and fats and the non-polar tail group forms hydrogen bonds with water.
The non-polar tail group forms dispersion forces with oil and fats, as well as forming dipole–dipole forces with water.
The polar head group forms dipole–dipole forces with oil, fats and water.
The polar head group forms ion–dipole forces with water and the non-polar tail group forms dispersion forces with oil and fats.

questions.question:
Which of the following is correct about the laboratory production of alcohol by the process of fermentation?

| | Requires oxygen | Produces oxygen | Suitable temperature ($^\circ$C) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Yes | No | 60 |
| B | No | Yes | 60 |
| C | No | No | 30 |
| D | Yes | No | 30 |
questions.answer: Fermentation of glucose by yeast, $C_6H_{12}O_6\to2C_2H_5OH+2CO_2$, is anaerobic (no oxygen required) and produces $CO_2$, not $O_2$. The enzymes in yeast work best at about $30$–$37^\circ$C and are denatured at $60^\circ$C (C).
options: Requires oxygen: yes; produces oxygen: no; $60^\circ$C
Requires oxygen: no; produces oxygen: yes; $60^\circ$C
Requires oxygen: no; produces oxygen: no; $30^\circ$C
Requires oxygen: yes; produces oxygen: no; $30^\circ$C

questions.question: A chemist synthesises a substance using the following pathway: $X\xrightarrow{\text{hydration}}Y\xrightarrow{\text{oxidation}}Z$. What are compounds $X$, $Y$ and $Z$?
questions.answer: Hydration is the addition of water across a $C=C$ double bond, so $X$ must be an alkene (prop-1-ene), not propane. Following Markovnikov's rule, hydration of prop-1-ene gives mainly propan-2-ol ($Y$). Oxidation of the secondary alcohol propan-2-ol gives the ketone propan-2-one (propanone) ($Z$) and cannot give a carboxylic acid (C).

questions.question: The graph shows the progress of an equilibrium reaction (reactants $\rightleftharpoons$ products): concentration of reactants (dashed line) and products (solid line) against time. Which row of the table correctly identifies what is happening at $t_1$, $t_2$ and $t_3$?
questions.answer: At $t_1$ both concentrations are constant, so the system is at equilibrium. At $t_2$ the concentration of the reactants suddenly jumps up and then falls, while the concentration of products rises to a higher level: reactants have been added and the system responds by shifting to the right. By $t_3$ the concentrations are constant again at a new equilibrium position (A).
options: $t_1$: at equilibrium; $t_2$: reactants added; $t_3$: new equilibrium position
$t_1$: at equilibrium; $t_2$: products added; $t_3$: new equilibrium position
$t_1$: no reaction occurring; $t_2$: reaction proceeding; $t_3$: reaction occurring
$t_1$: only forward reaction occurring; $t_2$: forward and reverse reactions occurring; $t_3$: only reverse reaction occurring

questions.question: The energy profile for the equilibrium reaction $2NO_2(g)\rightleftharpoons N_2O_4(g)$ is shown. The activation energies of the forward and reverse directions are
questions.answer: The activation energy of the forward reaction is the energy difference from the reactants ($2NO_2$ at about $0$) to the top of the peak (about $116$ kJ mol$^{-1}$). The reverse activation energy is the difference from the products ($N_2O_4$, at about $-60$ kJ mol$^{-1}$) to the peak: $116-(-60)=176$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ (C).
options: Forward: 50 kJ mol$^{-1}$; reverse: 116 kJ mol$^{-1}$
Forward: 116 kJ mol$^{-1}$; reverse: 50 kJ mol$^{-1}$
Forward: 116 kJ mol$^{-1}$; reverse: 176 kJ mol$^{-1}$
Forward: 176 kJ mol$^{-1}$; reverse: 116 kJ mol$^{-1}$

questions.question: The structural formulae of five organic compounds, labelled A–E, are shown (A is methyl propanoate, B is ethyl ethanoate, C is 2-methylpropanoic acid, D is propyl methanoate and E is butanoic acid). Which alternative below identifies a pair of these compounds as examples of each type of isomer?
questions.answer: Functional group isomers have the same molecular formula but different functional groups: C (a carboxylic acid) and D (an ester) are such a pair. Position isomers have the same functional group in a different position or arrangement: A (methyl propanoate) and B (ethyl ethanoate) are both esters with the ester linkage in a different position in the carbon chain (B). In the other options the first pair (C and E, A and B) are the same family, and B and C are not the same family.
options: Functional group isomers: C and E; position isomers: B and D
Functional group isomers: C and D; position isomers: A and B
Functional group isomers: A and B; position isomers: A and B
Functional group isomers: B and E; position isomers: B and C
