questions.question: Calculate the pH of a solution prepared by mixing 300 mL of 0.10 M HF and 200 mL of 0.10 M KOH. The $K_a$ of HF at $25^\circ\text{C}$ is $6.8\times10^{-4}$.
questions.answer: $n(\text{HF})=0.10\times0.300=0.030$ mol and $n(\text{OH}^-)=0.10\times0.200=0.020$ mol. After neutralisation: $n(\text{HF})=0.010$ mol and $n(\text{F}^-)=0.020$ mol, a buffer in 0.500 L: $[\text{HF}]=0.020$ M, $[\text{F}^-]=0.040$ M. $[\text{H}^+]=K_a\dfrac{[\text{HF}]}{[\text{F}^-]}=6.8\times10^{-4}\times\dfrac{0.020}{0.040}=3.4\times10^{-4}$ M, so $\text{pH}=3.47$, closest to 3.44 (D). Note: the school's worked solution ignores the neutralisation, treating the remaining HF alone (pH 2.4), which is incorrect; the answer is D.

questions.question: A 20.00 mL sample of vinegar is placed in a volumetric flask. The volumetric flask is then filled up to the line marking its designated volume. Then a 20.00 mL aliquot of the diluted sample of vinegar is titrated against a 0.102 M solution of potassium hydroxide using a phenolphthalein indicator. If the undiluted sample of vinegar has a concentration of 3.16% m/v acetic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, which volumetric flask should be selected to be able to dilute the original sample of vinegar and obtain titres of about 20 mL?
questions.answer: For a 20 mL titre: $n(\text{KOH})=0.102\times0.020=2.04\times10^{-3}$ mol $=n(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH})$ in the 20.00 mL aliquot, so the diluted vinegar is $0.102$ M, or $0.102\times60.05=6.12\ \text{g L}^{-1}=0.612\%$ m/v. The dilution factor needed is $\dfrac{3.16}{0.612}=5.2$, so 20.00 mL diluted to about 100 mL (A).

questions.question: The concentrations of reactants and products in a chemical reaction carried out at $25^\circ\text{C}$ for the dissociation of ammonia are $[\text{N}_2]=0.1$ M, $[\text{H}_2]=0.2$ M and $[\text{NH}_3]=0.3$ M. Calculate the equilibrium constant for this reaction. Show all relevant steps in your answer.
questions.answer: $2\text{NH}_3(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{N}_2(g)+3\text{H}_2(g)$. $K_{eq}=\dfrac{[\text{N}_2][\text{H}_2]^3}{[\text{NH}_3]^2}=\dfrac{(0.1)(0.2)^3}{(0.3)^2}=8.9\times10^{-3}$.

questions.question: How did Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples use their knowledge of solubility equilibria to remove toxins in cycad fruit?
questions.answer: The seeds of the cycad fruit are used to make bread but contain the water-soluble toxin cycasin. The seeds were sliced or crushed to increase the surface area, then placed in a woven bag or basket in running water for several hours or days (leaching). The toxin dissolves in the water: $\text{cycasin}(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{cycasin}(aq)$. The running water continually carries the dissolved toxin away, so this is an open system and the concentration of dissolved toxin in the water stays low. By Le Chatelier's principle, the equilibrium keeps shifting to the right (towards dissolving) and equilibrium is never reached, so eventually all the toxin dissolves out of the seeds, making them safe to eat.

questions.question: Part of the contact process for the manufacture of sulfuric acid is $2\text{SO}_2(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{SO}_3(g)$, $\Delta H=-192\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. A container was filled with an equilibrium mixture of sulfur dioxide, sulfur trioxide and oxygen in the presence of a catalyst, at $450^\circ\text{C}$. The graph shows concentrations of X, Y and $\text{O}_2$ over time. What change occurred at the 10-minute point?
questions.answer: Oxygen was added to the container: the concentration of $\text{O}_2$ increased instantly (a vertical spike) at 10 minutes.

questions.question: Part of the contact process is $2\text{SO}_2(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{SO}_3(g)$. At 10 minutes oxygen is added to an equilibrium mixture, after which X increases and Y decreases until 20 minutes. Which components of the equilibrium mixture are represented by X and Y?
questions.answer: X is $\text{SO}_3$ (its concentration increases as the equilibrium shifts right) and Y is $\text{SO}_2$ (its concentration decreases as it is consumed).

questions.question: For $2\text{SO}_2(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{SO}_3(g)$, $\Delta H=-192\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, oxygen is added to an equilibrium mixture at 10 minutes. Give explanations, using Le Chatelier's principle, for the changes in concentration that occurred in $\text{SO}_3$, $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ between 10 and 20 minutes (a new equilibrium is reached at 20 minutes).
questions.answer: Le Chatelier's principle states that when a change is imposed on a system at equilibrium, the position of equilibrium shifts in the direction that counteracts the change. The added $\text{O}_2$ increased $[\text{O}_2]$ suddenly, so the equilibrium shifts right to use up some of the extra $\text{O}_2$. The forward reaction rate temporarily exceeds the reverse rate, so $[\text{SO}_3]$ increases, $[\text{SO}_2]$ decreases, and $[\text{O}_2]$ falls after its initial spike (although not back to its original value) until a new equilibrium is reached at 20 minutes.

questions.question: For the reaction $2\text{SO}_2(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{SO}_3(g)$, $\Delta H=-192\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, account for TWO changes to the reaction conditions that would increase the rate of formation of $\text{SO}_3$ gas, and explain why the industrial production of $\text{SO}_3$ occurs at $450^\circ\text{C}$ and not at a lower or higher temperature.
questions.answer:
Increasing the pressure (reducing the volume) increases the concentrations of the gases, so there are more collisions per second and more successful collisions, and the equilibrium also shifts right (towards fewer moles of gas: 3 mol to 2 mol), increasing the rate and yield of $\text{SO}_3$. Adding a catalyst (or increasing the concentration of reactants, or removing product) increases the rate by providing a lower activation energy pathway so that a greater proportion of collisions are successful. (Raising the temperature also increases the rate, as particles have more kinetic energy and collide more often with sufficient energy.)

The forward reaction is exothermic, so by Le Chatelier's principle a lower temperature favours the forward reaction and gives a higher equilibrium yield of $\text{SO}_3$, while a higher temperature shifts the equilibrium left and reduces the yield (even though the rate increases). At a lower temperature, the rate would be too slow to produce the product in an acceptable time. $450^\circ\text{C}$ is the compromise at which the rate is high enough and the yield is still sufficiently high.

questions.question: Two students set up a simple game involving 40 individual paper clips. Student X connects individual paper clips into pairs, while Student Y takes apart the connected pairs. Both students are blindfolded. After a while, the numbers of individual and connected paper clips become constant. A third student then adds another pile of individual paper clips to the game, and after a while the numbers of individual and connected paper clips become constant again. By referring to the collision theory, explain how the addition of more paper clips to the game simulates the effect of concentration on a chemical equilibrium.
questions.answer:
The game models a closed system at dynamic equilibrium. Student X connecting paper clips represents the forward reaction (reactants $\rightarrow$ product) and Student Y separating them represents the reverse reaction. The numbers are constant when the rates of connecting and separating are equal, so the amounts of each stay constant even though both processes continue.

By collision theory, a reaction occurs when particles collide with enough energy and the correct orientation. Adding more individual paper clips is like increasing the concentration of reactant: with more reactant particles in the same space, there are more collisions per second, so Student X finds individual clips to connect more often and the forward reaction rate increases (the rate of connecting is now greater than the rate of separating). As a result, the number of connected pairs increases and the number of individual paper clips decreases (the equilibrium shifts towards the product).

As the pool of individual clips falls and the pairs increase, the forward rate decreases and the reverse rate increases until the two are equal again. A new equilibrium is established with constant numbers, with more connected pairs than before, just as increasing the concentration of a reactant in a chemical equilibrium shifts the position of equilibrium to the right until the rates are equal again.

questions.question: A student was given four colourless liquids labelled A, B, C and D, known to be ethanol, ethanoic acid, pentane and hex-3-ene, but the exact identity of each was unknown. Results: A is insoluble in water, decolourises red bromine solution and does not react with sodium carbonate solution. B is soluble in water, has no immediate reaction with bromine solution and evolves a gas with sodium carbonate solution. C is soluble in water and shows no reaction with bromine or sodium carbonate. D is insoluble in water and shows no reaction with bromine or sodium carbonate. Identify each of the liquids.
questions.answer: A is hex-3-ene (the only alkene, which decolourises bromine). B is ethanoic acid (the only acid, which reacts with carbonate to form $\text{CO}_2$ gas). C is ethanol (soluble in water, neutral, unreactive with bromine and carbonate). D is pentane (insoluble, saturated, so does not react with bromine).

questions.question: Hex-3-ene decolourises red-coloured bromine solution. Identify the type of reaction occurring between hex-3-ene and bromine solution, write a balanced equation and draw the structure(s) of the compound(s) formed.
questions.answer: It is an addition reaction, in which $\text{Br}_2$ adds across the carbon–carbon double bond: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}(l)+\text{Br}_2(aq)\rightarrow\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{Br}_2(l)$, i.e. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3+\text{Br}_2\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHBrCHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. The compound formed is 3,4-dibromohexane, a six-carbon chain with one bromine atom on each of carbons 3 and 4 (all single bonds); the red-brown colour disappears.

questions.question: Ethanoic acid reacts with sodium carbonate solution, evolving a gas. Identify the type of reaction occurring between ethanoic acid and $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ solution, write a balanced equation and draw the structure of the anion formed.
questions.answer: It is an acid–base (acid–carbonate) reaction: $2\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq)+\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)\rightarrow2\text{NaCH}_3\text{COO}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)+\text{CO}_2(g)$ (ionic: $2\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}+\text{CO}_3^{2-}\rightarrow2\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-+\text{H}_2\text{O}+\text{CO}_2$). The anion formed is the ethanoate ion, $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$: a methyl group bonded to a carbon that has one $\text{C}=\text{O}$ and one $\text{C-O}^-$ (the negative charge shared across the two oxygen atoms).

questions.question: Four colourless liquids are ethanol, ethanoic acid, pentane and hex-3-ene. Ethanol and ethanoic acid are soluble in water, while pentane and hex-3-ene are insoluble. Discuss the different solubilities of the four compounds in water.
questions.answer:
Pentane and hex-3-ene are non-polar hydrocarbons held together only by weak dispersion forces. Water is polar with strong hydrogen bonding between its molecules. Hydrocarbon molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, and the attraction between water molecules is much stronger than any attraction between water and the hydrocarbons, so they do not mix and form separate layers (they are insoluble).

Ethanol is polar: its $-\text{OH}$ group forms strong hydrogen bonds with water molecules. Its short non-polar hydrocarbon chain has no attraction for water, but the hydrogen bonding is strong enough that ethanol is fully miscible with water.

Ethanoic acid is polar: the $-\text{COOH}$ group forms hydrogen bonds with water (through the $\text{O-H}$ hydrogen and the oxygen atoms). It also partially ionises in water to form $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ ions, which are attracted to the polar water molecules. It dissolves readily and does not form layers.

questions.question: The white smoke reaction is a neutralisation reaction between the vapours of concentrated solutions of hydrochloric acid and ammonia, producing fine white salt crystals that are momentarily suspended in air. Justify why this reaction can only be explained by the Brønsted–Lowry definition of acids and bases and not the Arrhenius definition. Include a chemical equation in your answer.
questions.answer: $\text{HCl}(g)+\text{NH}_3(g)\rightarrow\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(s)$. In this reaction, $\text{HCl}$ donates a proton ($\text{H}^+$) to $\text{NH}_3$, which accepts it (forming $\text{NH}_4^+$): $\text{HCl}$ is a Brønsted–Lowry acid (proton donor) and $\text{NH}_3$ is a Brønsted–Lowry base (proton acceptor). The Arrhenius definition says that an acid produces $\text{H}^+$ ions and a base produces $\text{OH}^-$ ions in aqueous solution, so it requires water as the solvent. The reaction occurs between gases in the absence of water, and $\text{NH}_3$ does not contain or release $\text{OH}^-$ ions, so the Arrhenius definition cannot explain it.

questions.question: A small organic molecule contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and chlorine atoms. A pH probe was inserted into a dilute aqueous solution of this compound and the pH was 4.5. The infrared spectrum, mass spectrum, $^{1}$H NMR spectrum and $^{13}$C NMR spectrum are provided. Identify the two peaks on the infrared spectrum that correspond to the presence of two functional groups involving carbon, hydrogen and/or oxygen atoms in this compound (the C–Cl peak is labelled).
questions.answer: A broad, strong absorption at about $2500$–$3300\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ is the O–H stretch of a carboxylic acid, and a strong sharp peak at about $1700\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ is the C=O stretch (carbonyl) of the carboxylic acid group.

questions.question: A small organic molecule contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and chlorine atoms. A pH probe was inserted into a dilute aqueous solution of this compound and the pH was 4.5. The infrared spectrum, mass spectrum, $^{1}$H NMR spectrum and $^{13}$C NMR spectrum are provided. What information is provided by the pH of the aqueous solution?
questions.answer: A pH of 4.5 shows that the compound is acidic (it donates protons in water), so it contains a carboxylic acid ($-\text{COOH}$) group.

questions.question: A small organic molecule contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and chlorine atoms. A pH probe was inserted into a dilute aqueous solution of this compound and the pH was 4.5. The infrared spectrum, mass spectrum, $^{1}$H NMR spectrum and $^{13}$C NMR spectrum are provided. The mass spectrum shows two parent (molecular ion) peaks at $m/z$ 108 and 110 (relative intensities about 3:1). What information is provided by the mass spectrum?
questions.answer: The molecular mass is 108 or 110, depending on which chlorine isotope is present: $^{35}\text{Cl}$ gives the peak at 108 and $^{37}\text{Cl}$ the peak at 110, whose 3:1 ratio matches the natural abundance of the isotopes (75.8%:24.2%). This shows the molecule contains one chlorine atom and has a molecular mass of about 108.5.

questions.question: A small organic molecule contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and chlorine atoms. A pH probe was inserted into a dilute aqueous solution of this compound and the pH was 4.5. The infrared spectrum, mass spectrum, $^{1}$H NMR spectrum and $^{13}$C NMR spectrum are provided. The $^1$H NMR spectrum has three signals: $\delta=1.7$ ppm, doublet (2 peaks), relative area 3; $\delta=4.5$ ppm, quartet (4 peaks), relative area 1; $\delta=11.2$ ppm, singlet (1 peak), relative area 1. What specific information about the structure of the compound is provided by the splitting pattern in the $^1$H NMR spectrum and the data table?
questions.answer: There are three different hydrogen environments, in the ratio 3:1:1 (5 hydrogen atoms). By the $n+1$ rule, the quartet shows that one hydrogen environment (4.5 ppm, 1 H) has three neighbouring hydrogens on the adjacent carbon; the doublet shows that one environment (1.7 ppm, 3 H) has one neighbouring hydrogen; and the singlet shows one environment (11.2 ppm, 1 H) has no neighbouring hydrogens. Hence the groups are $\text{CH}_3$ (doublet), $\text{CH}$ (quartet) joined to each other, and a $\text{COOH}$ proton (singlet, 11.2 ppm), which is not coupled to others.

questions.question: A small organic molecule contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and chlorine atoms. A pH probe was inserted into a dilute aqueous solution of this compound and the pH was 4.5. The infrared spectrum, mass spectrum, $^{1}$H NMR spectrum and $^{13}$C NMR spectrum are provided. The mass spectrum shows parent peaks at $m/z$ 108 and 110 (one Cl atom), the $^{13}$C NMR spectrum has three signals (at about 175, 55 and 21 ppm), the $^1$H NMR spectrum has three environments in the ratio 3:1:1, and the compound is a carboxylic acid. Use the data provided to determine the number of carbon and hydrogen atoms in a molecule of this compound. Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: The molecular mass is 108 (with $^{35}\text{Cl}$). Subtracting one Cl (35) gives 73 for the remaining carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. The compound is an acid ($-\text{COOH}$, containing two oxygen atoms, 32), leaving $73-32=41$ for carbon and hydrogen. The $^{13}$C NMR shows three different carbon environments, so at least 3 carbons (36), leaving $41-36=5$ for hydrogen, which agrees with the relative areas $3+1+1=5$ hydrogen atoms in the $^1$H NMR. So the molecule has 3 carbon atoms and 5 hydrogen atoms, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_5\text{O}_2\text{Cl}$.

questions.question: A small organic molecule contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and chlorine atoms. A pH probe was inserted into a dilute aqueous solution of this compound and the pH was 4.5. The infrared spectrum, mass spectrum, $^{1}$H NMR spectrum and $^{13}$C NMR spectrum are provided. The molecule is $\text{C}_3\text{H}_5\text{O}_2\text{Cl}$, with a $\text{CH}_3$ group (doublet), a $\text{CH}$ (quartet) and a $\text{COOH}$ group. Draw a molecular structure for this molecule.
questions.answer: 2-chloropropanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{-CHCl-COOH}$: a $\text{CH}_3$ group bonded to a central $\text{CH}$ carbon, which carries the chlorine atom and is bonded to the carboxylic acid carbon ($\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{OH}$). The $\text{CH}$ has three $\text{CH}_3$ hydrogens as neighbours (quartet) and the $\text{CH}_3$ has one neighbouring hydrogen (doublet).

questions.question: Account for the cleaning action of soap by describing its structure and interaction with water.
questions.answer: A soap molecule is the sodium (or potassium) salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid: a long non-polar hydrocarbon chain with a negatively charged carboxylate group ($-\text{COO}^-\ \text{Na}^+$) at one end. The hydrocarbon tail is non-polar and hydrophobic (water-repelling) and is attracted to oil and grease by dispersion forces. The carboxylate head is charged and hydrophilic: it forms ion–dipole attractions and hydrogen bonds with polar water molecules. When soap is mixed with water and dirty (oily) material, the hydrophobic tails dissolve in the oil and the hydrophilic heads face the water. With agitation, the oil is broken into tiny droplets surrounded by soap molecules, forming micelles with the tails inside and the negatively charged heads outside. The negative charges on the outside repel each other, so the droplets stay dispersed (an emulsion) and can be rinsed away with the water.

questions.question: Three solutions of citric acid, hydrochloric acid and acetic (ethanoic) acid each have a concentration of $0.1\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ and a pH of 2.1, 1.0 and 2.9, respectively. Why are the pH values different even though the acid concentrations are the same?
questions.answer: pH $=-\log[\text{H}^+]$, so the pH depends on the hydrogen ion concentration, which depends on how far each acid ionises. $\text{HCl}$ is a strong acid and ionises completely, so $[\text{H}^+]=0.1$ M and pH is 1.0. Citric acid and acetic acid are weak acids and only partially ionise (in equilibrium), giving lower $[\text{H}^+]$ and higher pH. Citric acid ionises to a greater extent than acetic acid (it is the stronger weak acid, with a larger $K_a$), so its pH of 2.1 is lower than 2.9.

questions.question: A student dilutes 0.1 M acetic (ethanoic) acid by dissolving 10 mL in 100 mL of water. The pH of the original solution is 2.9 and the diluted solution's pH was measured to be 3.4. They expect that decreasing the concentration of hydrogen ions by a factor of 10 will increase the pH by one unit. Account for the increase in pH of only 0.5 units. Use a chemical equation to support your answer.
questions.answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq)+\text{H}^+(aq)$. Since $\text{pH}=-\log[\text{H}^+]$, a tenfold decrease in $[\text{H}^+]$ would increase the pH by exactly 1 (to 3.9) if the acid were strong and fully ionised. Acetic acid is a weak acid in equilibrium. Dilution decreases the concentration of all the species, and by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts to the right (towards the side with more particles/moles, producing more ions) to partly counteract the decrease, so more acid molecules ionise and some extra $\text{H}^+$ is produced. Therefore $[\text{H}^+]$ falls by less than a factor of 10, and the pH rises by only about 0.5 units.

questions.question: Hydrogen and carbon monoxide react as gases: $2\text{H}_2(g)+\text{CO}(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{OH}(g)$. 1.0 mol of $\text{H}_2$ and 1.0 mol of CO were placed into a 4.0 L container at 298 K. When the system had reached equilibrium, it was found that 0.2 mol of $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ had been formed. Calculate the equilibrium constant for the reaction under these conditions.
questions.answer: Initial: $[\text{H}_2]=[\text{CO}]=0.25$ M. Change: $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ forms $+0.050$ M (0.2 mol in 4.0 L), so $\text{CO}$ changes by $-0.050$ M and $\text{H}_2$ by $-0.10$ M. Equilibrium: $[\text{H}_2]=0.15$ M, $[\text{CO}]=0.20$ M, $[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]=0.050$ M. $K_{eq}=\dfrac{[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]}{[\text{H}_2]^2[\text{CO}]}=\dfrac{0.050}{(0.15)^2(0.20)}=11$.

questions.question: An investigation was carried out to analyse a commercial lawn fertiliser. A 1.00 g sample of fertiliser containing 24.0% sulfur (S) in the form of sulfate ($\text{SO}_4^{2-}$) was dissolved in water. 100 mL of $0.20\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ barium chloride solution was then added and a precipitate formed. Calculate the theoretical percentage by mass of sulfate ($\text{SO}_4^{2-}$) in the fertiliser.
questions.answer: $\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq)+\text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq)\rightarrow\text{BaSO}_4(s)$. The mass of S in the sample is $0.240$ g, so $n(\text{S})=\dfrac{0.240}{32.07}=7.48\times10^{-3}$ mol $=n(\text{SO}_4^{2-})$ (one S per sulfate). $m(\text{SO}_4^{2-})=7.48\times10^{-3}\times96.07=0.719$ g, so the percentage by mass of sulfate is $\dfrac{0.719}{1.00}\times100=71.9\%$. (The $\text{BaCl}_2$ is in excess: $0.020$ mol of $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ against $7.48\times10^{-3}$ mol of sulfate, so all the sulfate precipitates as $\text{BaSO}_4$.)

questions.question: Nylon 6-6 is a condensation polymer formed from hexane-1,6-diamine ($\text{NH}_2\text{-C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{-NH}_2$, molar mass $116.20\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) and hexanedioic acid ($\text{COOH-C}_4\text{H}_8\text{-COOH}$, molar mass $146.14\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) according to $n\,\text{NH}_2\text{-C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{-NH}_2+n\,\text{COOH-C}_4\text{H}_8\text{-COOH}\rightarrow n\,\text{COOH-C}_4\text{H}_8\text{-CO-NH-C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{-NH}_2+(2n-1)\text{H}_2\text{O}$. The molar mass of nylon 6-6 (per mole of the unit shown) is $244.31\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. If 220.0 g of hexanedioic acid and 280.0 g of hexane-1,6-diamine are reacted together in a vessel, what mass of nylon 6-6 is produced if the reaction goes to completion?
questions.answer: $n(\text{hexanedioic acid})=\dfrac{220.0}{146.14}=1.505$ mol and $n(\text{diamine})=\dfrac{280.0}{116.20}=2.410$ mol. The reaction is 1:1, so hexanedioic acid is the limiting reagent. $n(\text{nylon})=1.505$ mol, so $m=1.505\times244.31=367.8$ g (using the molar mass given). Note: $244.31$ is the molar mass of a repeat unit plus one $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (the formula as written), so for a long polymer chain the mass is closer to $1.505\times226.3\approx341$ g (the repeat unit $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{N}_2\text{O}_2$). The school's expected answer is 367.8 g.

questions.question: The fermentation of glucose is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6(aq)\rightarrow2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(aq)+2\text{CO}_2(g)$. A student added 12 g of glucose to a conical flask with 1 g of yeast and 50 mL of water at $37^\circ\text{C}$, on a balance connected to a computer. The graph shows the mass of the reaction mixture over 24 hours. Calculate the mass change in the conical flask by referring to the graph.
questions.answer: Initial mass about 128.68 g and final mass about 127.24 g: the mass change is $128.68-127.24=1.44$ g (accept $\pm0.04$ g), a mass loss as $\text{CO}_2$ escapes.

questions.question: The fermentation of glucose is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6(aq)\rightarrow2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(aq)+2\text{CO}_2(g)$. A student fermented 12 g of glucose in a flask on a balance, and the mass of the flask decreased by 1.44 g (as $\text{CO}_2$ escaped). Calculate the mass of ethanol produced by the reaction and compare this to the theoretical yield of ethanol. Show all working.
questions.answer:
Actual: $n(\text{CO}_2)=\dfrac{1.44}{44.01}=0.0327$ mol; $n(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH})=0.0327$ mol (1:1 ratio), so $m=0.0327\times46.07=1.5$ g.

Theoretical: $n(\text{glucose})=\dfrac{12}{180.16}=0.0666$ mol; $n(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH})=2\times0.0666=0.133$ mol; $m=0.133\times46.07=6.1$ g.

The actual mass of ethanol (1.5 g) is much lower than the theoretical mass (6.1 g): a yield of about 25%.

questions.question: Three organic compounds have the following formulae and properties: Q, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ (molecular weight 74.08, boiling point $141.2^\circ\text{C}$, $pK_a$ 4.88); R, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ (73.14, $78^\circ\text{C}$, $pK_a$ 10.21); S, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$ (73.09, $213^\circ\text{C}$, $pK_a$ 0.42). Name the compounds Q, R and S.
questions.answer: Q is propanoic acid, R is butan-1-amine (butylamine) and S is propanamide.

questions.question: Three organic compounds of similar molecular mass are propanoic acid Q, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ (boiling point $141.2^\circ\text{C}$), butan-1-amine R, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ ($78^\circ\text{C}$), and propanamide S, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$ ($213^\circ\text{C}$). Explain the variations in boiling points between compounds Q, R and S.
questions.answer:
All three have similar molar masses (about 73–74 g mol$^{-1}$), so their dispersion forces are similar. The differences are due to the strength of the other intermolecular forces due to the functional groups. The stronger the intermolecular forces, the more energy is needed to overcome them, and the higher the boiling point.

The amide S has the highest boiling point: the $\text{N-H}$ and $\text{C=O}$ bonds are both very polar, giving strong hydrogen bonding between molecules (including pairs of molecules, with $\text{N-H}\cdots\text{O=C}$ bonds in each direction, giving closer packing and stronger hydrogen bonds), so the most energy is needed to separate the molecules.

The carboxylic acid Q has a lower boiling point than the amide, but higher than the amine: it forms hydrogen bonds through its highly polar $\text{O-H}$ bond (and the $\text{C=O}$). The $\text{O-H}$ bond is more polar than $\text{N-H}$ because oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen, so its hydrogen bonds are stronger than those of the amine.

The amine R has the lowest boiling point: it can form hydrogen bonds through $\text{N-H}$, but these are weaker as nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, and it has only one hydrogen-bonding group.

questions.question: The phosphate buffer system operates in the internal fluid of cells. The pH of an equimolar solution of sodium dihydrogen phosphate, $\text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_4$, and disodium hydrogen phosphate, $\text{Na}_2\text{HPO}_4$, is 6.8. Write a chemical equation that represents the equilibrium system described.
questions.answer: $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)+\text{HPO}_4^{2-}(aq)$

questions.question: An equimolar solution of sodium dihydrogen phosphate, $\text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_4$, and disodium hydrogen phosphate, $\text{Na}_2\text{HPO}_4$, has a pH of 6.8 and is a buffer. The equilibrium is $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)+\text{HPO}_4^{2-}(aq)$. Explain how this system operates as a buffer and account for what would happen if a small volume of $0.1\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ carbonic acid, $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$, was added to the solution.
questions.answer:
The mixture contains a weak acid ($\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$) and its conjugate base ($\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$) in high concentrations, so it resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added. Added acid is neutralised by the conjugate base, and added base is neutralised by the weak acid, with the equilibrium shifting (Le Chatelier's principle) to minimise the change.

Adding a small volume of carbonic acid briefly increases $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$. By Le Chatelier's principle, the equilibrium shifts left: the extra $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ reacts with the large reserve of $\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$, forming more $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ and removing most of the added $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$. Since $[\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-]$ and $[\text{HPO}_4^{2-}]$ change only slightly, their ratio, and therefore the pH, remains approximately constant at 6.8.

questions.question: A sample of lemon juice was analysed in the laboratory. A student took 25.00 mL of the juice and diluted it to 250.00 mL. Exactly 25.00 mL of the diluted lemon juice was titrated with a standardised $0.1245\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide solution using phenolphthalein as the indicator. An average titre of 23.95 mL of sodium hydroxide was required. Assuming that the lemon juice contained only citric acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_7$), calculate the concentration in $\text{mol L}^{-1}$ of citric acid in the undiluted lemon juice. Note: citric acid is a triprotic acid.
questions.answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_7(aq)+3\text{NaOH}(aq)\rightarrow\text{Na}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7(aq)+3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$. $n(\text{NaOH})=0.1245\times0.02395=2.981\times10^{-3}$ mol. $n(\text{citric acid})=\dfrac13\times2.981\times10^{-3}=9.939\times10^{-4}$ mol in the 25.00 mL aliquot. $c(\text{diluted})=\dfrac{9.939\times10^{-4}}{0.02500}=0.03976$ M. The dilution was $25.00\to250.00$ mL (tenfold), so $c(\text{undiluted})=0.3976\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ (0.398 M).

questions.question: Compare the molar solubility of solid $\text{CaF}_2$ ($K_{sp}=4\times10^{-11}$) in a $0.025$ M $\text{NaF}$ solution to the solubility in distilled water.
questions.answer:
$\text{CaF}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ca}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{F}^-(aq)$, $K_{sp}=[\text{Ca}^{2+}][\text{F}^-]^2$.

In distilled water: let the molar solubility be $s$, so $[\text{Ca}^{2+}]=s$ and $[\text{F}^-]=2s$: $K_{sp}=s(2s)^2=4s^3=4\times10^{-11}$, so $s=2.2\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

In 0.025 M $\text{NaF}$: $[\text{F}^-]=0.025+2s\approx0.025$ M (the common ion; $2s$ is negligible), so $K_{sp}=s(0.025)^2=4\times10^{-11}$ and $s=\dfrac{4\times10^{-11}}{6.25\times10^{-4}}=6.4\times10^{-8}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

The molar solubility of $\text{CaF}_2$ in 0.025 M $\text{NaF}$ ($6.4\times10^{-8}$ M) is about 3000 times lower than in water ($2.2\times10^{-4}$ M), because the common ion $\text{F}^-$ shifts the equilibrium to the left (Le Chatelier's principle).

questions.question: Which of the reagents will dehydrate an alcohol to an alkene?
questions.answer: Concentrated sulfuric acid is a dehydrating agent that removes water from an alcohol (elimination) to form an alkene (D). Acidified permanganate oxidises alcohols and bromine water reacts with alkenes; dilute acid contains too much water.

questions.question: Which compound is a functional group isomer of pentan-2-one?
questions.answer: Pentan-2-one is $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ (a ketone). A functional group isomer has the same formula but a different functional group: pentanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, an aldehyde (B). A and D are the ketone pentan-2-one and 3-methylbutan-2-one (not functional group isomers), and C is an ester with a different formula.

questions.question: The structure of a compound is shown. What is the IUPAC preferred name for this compound?
questions.answer: The structure is a five-carbon chain: $\text{CHF}_2-\text{CHCl}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}_3$. The principal functional group (OH) gets the lowest number, so number from the $\text{CH}_3$ end: OH on C2, Cl on C4, two F on C5. Substituents are listed alphabetically: 4-chloro-5,5-difluoropentan-2-ol (D).

questions.question: A student was carrying out an experiment to isolate the components of a solution containing iodide, carbonate, and sulfate ions using precipitation reactions. Which of the following reagents would be invalid for this procedure?
questions.answer: Sulfuric acid would react with carbonate ($\text{CO}_3^{2-}+2\text{H}^+\rightarrow\text{H}_2\text{O}+\text{CO}_2$), destroying it, and would add extra sulfate ions that would interfere with the sulfate in the sample (A). The others are suitable: nitric acid can be used to dissolve carbonate precipitates, silver nitrate precipitates the halide, and magnesium nitrate precipitates carbonate.

questions.question: The diagram shows the key components in a UV-Visible spectrophotometer. When the instrument is operated to measure the absorbance of a sample, the intensity of light is recorded at two different locations. Which pair of measurements is subtracted to find the light absorption?
questions.answer: Absorbance depends on the intensity of light entering the sample (Y, after the monochromator's exit slit) compared with the intensity leaving the sample (Z, at the detector). The light absorbed is $Y-Z$ (C).

questions.question: Which molecule has a linear shape?
questions.answer: Ethyne ($\text{HC}\equiv\text{CH}$) has a triple bond, so each carbon has two regions of electron density and a bond angle of $180^\circ$ (linear) (A). Ethene is planar ($120^\circ$); ethane and methane are tetrahedral ($109.5^\circ$ at each carbon).

questions.question: The graph shows a conductivity titration graph. Which type of acid-base titration is illustrated with the shape of this graph?
questions.answer: The conductance falls as the highly conducting $\text{H}^+$ is neutralised, then levels off after the equivalence point because the excess weak base is only slightly ionised and adds few ions (B). A strong base would cause a sharp increase after the equivalence point (as in strong acid vs strong base, which shows a V-shape). A weak acid starts with low conductance.

questions.question: Which of the following would turn pink litmus blue?
questions.answer: Pink (acidic) litmus turns blue in a basic solution. Methylamine, $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$, is an amine, a weak base that accepts a proton from water, forming $\text{OH}^-$ (D). The alkane, alcohol and ester are neutral.

questions.question: Which of the following salt solutions would give a blue grey flame colour?
questions.answer: Lead ions give a blue-grey (pale blue-white) flame (A). Copper gives green/blue-green, barium gives pale green and calcium gives orange-red.

questions.question: Dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) is introduced into a sealed vessel and left to reach equilibrium according to $\text{CO}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{CO}_2(g)$. Which of the following changes to the system is consistent with the shift to the equilibrium?
questions.answer: Adding gaseous $\text{CO}_2$ increases the concentration of the product, so the system shifts left (towards the solid) to partly counteract the change (C). Doubling the volume would shift right (the pressure of gas falls), raising the temperature favours the endothermic sublimation (shifts right), and adding more of a pure solid does not change the position of equilibrium.
options: Doubling of reaction volume: system shifts left
Increase of reaction temperature: no change
Addition of more gaseous $\text{CO}_2$: system shifts left
Addition of more dry ice: system shifts right

questions.question: Two solutions of the same concentration, Y and Z, had pH measurements of 2.00 and 4.00 respectively. Which statement about solutions Y and Z is correct?
questions.answer: $[\text{H}^+]_Y=10^{-2}$ M and $[\text{H}^+]_Z=10^{-4}$ M, so Y has 100 times the $[\text{H}^+]$ of Z (D). Correspondingly $[\text{OH}^-]$ in Z is 100 times that in Y.
options: The concentration of $\text{OH}^-$ in solution Z is 10 times greater than the concentration of $\text{OH}^-$ in solution Y.
The concentration of $\text{OH}^-$ in solution Z is two times greater than the concentration of $\text{OH}^-$ in solution Y.
The concentration of $\text{H}^+$ in solution Y is two times greater than the concentration of $\text{H}^+$ in solution Z.
The concentration of $\text{H}^+$ in solution Y is 100 times greater than the concentration of $\text{H}^+$ in solution Z.

questions.question: Glycine is an amino acid that can undergo condensation polymerisation. What is the molar mass of the polymer formed from 1000 glycine monomer units?
questions.answer: Glycine, $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{COOH}$, has $M=75.07\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. Joining 1000 units releases 999 molecules of water: $M=1000\times75.07-999\times18.016=7.507\times10^4-1.800\times10^4=5.7\times10^4\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ (C).

questions.question: A student has three dropper bottles containing: A, sodium carbonate, 0.0001 M; B, silver sulfate, 0.001 M; C, lead chloride, 0.0005 M. The student places a plastic sheet on a black bench and combines a drop from two different dropper bottles (A+B, A+C and B+C). How many of the three combinations would show ‘No visible reaction’?
questions.answer: In each case a precipitate forms: A+B gives silver carbonate ($\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3$, $K_{sp}\approx8\times10^{-12}$; after mixing $Q\approx(1\times10^{-3})^2(5\times10^{-5})=5\times10^{-11}>K_{sp}$), A+C gives lead carbonate ($\text{PbCO}_3$) and B+C gives silver chloride ($\text{AgCl}$, and lead sulfate). So no combination is without a visible reaction: 0 (A).

questions.question: The gas-phase reaction $\text{H}_2(g)+\text{I}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{HI}(g)$ has $K=46$. 0.22 mol of hydrogen, 0.63 mol of iodine and 2.40 mol of hydrogen iodide were added to a 110 L container. Which of the following correctly identifies the relationship between $Q$ and $K$ and the equilibrium shift?
questions.answer: Since the number of moles of gas is the same on both sides, the volume cancels: $Q=\dfrac{[\text{HI}]^2}{[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]}=\dfrac{2.40^2}{0.22\times0.63}=41.6$. $Q<K=46$, so the reaction shifts right to form more product (B).

questions.question: An experiment measures the temperature change for a heat of combustion reaction. 100.0 mL of water at 308 K was heated by the burning of 1.05 g of ethanol in the spirit burner. Only 45.0% of the energy produced was used to heat the water. The molar heat of combustion of ethanol is $-1367\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. What is the final temperature of the water?
questions.answer: $n(\text{ethanol})=\dfrac{1.05}{46.068}=0.02279$ mol; energy $=0.02279\times1367=31.2$ kJ; energy to the water $=0.450\times31.2=14.0$ kJ. $\Delta T=\dfrac{14.0\times10^3}{100.0\times4.18}=33.6$ K. The initial temperature is $308\ \text{K}=34.85^\circ\text{C}$, so the final temperature is $34.85+33.6\approx68.5^\circ\text{C}$ (C).

questions.question: A molecule of 2-chlorobutanal is shown, with an arrow pointing to the hydrogen on carbon 2 (the carbon bonded to the chlorine). Which of the following shows the splitting pattern observed for the labelled environment in the proton NMR spectrum for this molecule?
questions.answer: The labelled hydrogen is on C2, which is bonded to C1 (the aldehyde carbon, 1 H) and C3 ($\text{CH}_2$, 2 H). It has $1+2=3$ neighbouring hydrogens, so by the $n+1$ rule it splits into a quartet (C).

questions.question: An investigation using gravimetric analysis was carried out to determine the identity of an anion in a solution. Adding 0.04 mol of silver ions resulted in the production of 5.52 g of precipitate. Which of the following is a possible identity for the anion?
questions.answer: Calculate the molar mass of the precipitate for each option: $\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3$: $n=0.02$ mol, $m=0.02\times275.75=5.51$ g (matches); AgBr: $0.04\times187.77=7.51$ g; AgI: $0.04\times234.77=9.39$ g; $\text{Ag}_3\text{PO}_4$: $\dfrac{0.04}{3}\times418.58=5.58$ g. 5.52 g is closest to the carbonate (A).

questions.question: An organic molecule with the chemical formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}$ gives the mass spectrum shown (molecular ion at $m/z$ 58, base peak at $m/z$ 43). Which of the following would give the mass spectrum shown?
questions.answer: The base peak at $m/z$ 43 is $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^+$ ($12\times2+3+16=43$), formed by losing a methyl group from propanone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$ (B). Propanal would fragment mainly to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^+$ ($m/z$ 29) and $\text{CHO}^+$ ($m/z$ 29), and the enols are unstable.

questions.question: 25.0 mL of a $1.00\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide solution in a conical flask is titrated against $1.00\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid solution. What volume of hydrochloric acid must be added to achieve a pH of 1 in the mixture?
questions.answer: pH 1 means $[\text{H}^+]=0.10$ M. With $V$ mL of acid added, excess $\text{H}^+=\dfrac{V-25.0}{V+25.0}\times1.00=0.10$, so $V-25.0=0.10V+2.5$ and $V=30.6$ mL. The closest option is 30.0 mL (C).

questions.question: An investigation determined the amount of manganese in a sample of fertiliser. 5.67 g of the fertiliser was dissolved and treated to perform $\text{Mn}^{2+}(aq)+4\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightarrow\text{MnO}_4^-(aq)+8\text{H}^+(aq)+5e^-$. The resulting permanganate solution was transferred to a 100 mL volumetric flask and filled to the mark. A sample gave an absorbance of 0.45 in a colorimeter, and was compared with the calibration curve provided. What is the percentage mass of manganese ions in the fertiliser sample?
questions.answer: From the calibration curve, an absorbance of 0.45 corresponds to $[\text{MnO}_4^-]\approx2.25\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$. $n=2.25\times10^{-4}\times0.100=2.25\times10^{-5}$ mol $=n(\text{Mn}^{2+})$. $m=2.25\times10^{-5}\times54.94=1.24\times10^{-3}$ g, so $\%=\dfrac{1.24\times10^{-3}}{5.67}\times100=0.022\%\approx0.02\%$ (A).

questions.question: But-2-ene undergoes an addition reaction with water. Give the name and structural formula of the product of this reaction.
questions.answer: Water adds across the double bond: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. The product is butan-2-ol: a four-carbon chain with an $-\text{OH}$ group on carbon 2.

questions.question: A chemist has proposed the integration of an electrochemical cell into the well-established Haber-Bosch process used for the industrial synthesis of ammonia. This would replace the conventional temperature and pressure system, which is driven by the combustion of fossil fuels. An overview of the design is presented in the diagram (a PCMR cell fed with methane/biogas and steam, producing $\text{CO}_2$/$\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and ammonia, and a PCFC cell fed with air that generates electricity and recycles $\text{N}_2$/$\text{H}_2$). Using the diagram, explain TWO advantages associated with the use of electrochemical cells in this process.
questions.answer:
Advantage 1: the electrochemical cells allow the use of renewable energy (solar and wind electricity) and renewable reagents (biogas) in place of fossil fuels. This avoids the large pollution (greenhouse gas emissions) from burning fossil fuels for high temperature and pressure and conserves a finite resource.

Advantage 2: the two cells allow recycling of chemicals and electricity. Unreacted $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$ are returned to the PCMR cell, and the PCFC cell generates electricity that is used to power the PCMR cell. This reduces the costs of reagents and of external electrical energy, and improves the efficiency (yield) of the process.

questions.question: Determine how many grams of calcium sulfate will dissolve in 100.0 mL of a $0.0020\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ solution of sodium sulfate. ($K_{sp}(\text{CaSO}_4)=4.93\times10^{-5}$)

Consider the reaction at equilibrium: $\text{N}_2\text{O}_5(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{NO}_3(g)+\text{NO}_2(g)$. Le Chatelier's principle and collision theory can both be used to understand the behaviour of equilibrium systems. Show how both of these can be used to explain the change that occurs to the system when some $\text{NO}_3(g)$ is removed.
questions.answer:
Le Chatelier's principle states that when a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change, the system shifts to partially counteract the change. $\text{NO}_3(g)$, a product, is removed, so the position shifts to the right to form more $\text{NO}_3$ until a new equilibrium is reached.

Collision theory: reaction rates depend on the number of successful collisions per second. At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal. When some $\text{NO}_3$ is removed, there are fewer $\text{NO}_3$ molecules to collide with $\text{NO}_2$, so the rate of the reverse reaction decreases immediately, while the forward rate is initially unchanged. The forward rate is therefore greater than the reverse rate, and there is a net shift right. As this occurs, $[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]$ falls, so the forward rate decreases, and $[\text{NO}_3]$ rises, so the reverse rate increases, until the two rates are again equal and a new equilibrium is established.

questions.question: An analytical chemist added 2.56 g of barium hydroxide to 0.250 L of a $0.200\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ solution of nitric acid in a 400 mL beaker. Calculate the pH of the resulting solution. Assume the total volume remains unchanged.
Explain how nitric acid meets the criteria for the Arrhenius and Brønsted–Lowry models of acids. Use equations to support your answer.
questions.answer:
An Arrhenius acid is a substance that ionises in water to produce hydrogen (hydronium) ions: $\text{HNO}_3(aq)\rightarrow\text{H}^+(aq)+\text{NO}_3^-(aq)$. Nitric acid is a strong acid, so it ionises completely (one-way arrow).

A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton donor. $\text{HNO}_3(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightarrow\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)+\text{NO}_3^-(aq)$. Here $\text{HNO}_3$ (acid) donates a proton to $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (base), forming the conjugate acid $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ and the conjugate base $\text{NO}_3^-$.

questions.question: Ethanol is produced through fermentation of glucose solution. The reaction is carried out in a school laboratory, and the volume of carbon dioxide generated is measured under standard laboratory conditions (25 °C and 100 kPa). Hours / total volume of $\text{CO}_2$ (mL): 0 / 0; 20 / 500; 40 / 760; 60 / 900; 80 / 960; 100 / 960; 120 / 960. Describe how the results would be plotted as a graph, including the line of best fit, and state the volume of $\text{CO}_2$ produced at 30 hours from your graph.
questions.answer: Plot time (hours) on the horizontal axis (0 to 120, scale 20 h per division) and total volume of $\text{CO}_2$ (mL) on the vertical axis (0 to 1000, with units), label both axes, plot the seven points accurately, and draw a smooth curve of best fit (not straight lines joining the points). The curve rises steeply from the origin, becomes less steep, and levels off at 960 mL from 80 hours (see the graph). At 30 hours the curve reads about 640 mL (accept 620–660 mL).

questions.question: Ethanol is produced through fermentation of glucose solution, with the total volume of $\text{CO}_2$ produced measured over time: 0 h: 0 mL; 20 h: 500 mL; 40 h: 760 mL; 60 h: 900 mL; 80 h: 960 mL; 100 h: 960 mL; 120 h: 960 mL. Explain the shape of the graph of volume against time.
questions.answer: The volume of $\text{CO}_2$ increases until it reaches a maximum of 960 mL and then plateaus, because all of the glucose has been used up (or the yeast has been killed by the concentration of ethanol), so no more $\text{CO}_2$ is produced. The graph is a curve, not a straight line, because the rate of reaction decreases as the reactants are used up: there are fewer reactant particles and so fewer successful collisions per second. The curve is steep at the start, when the concentration of glucose is highest, and gradually becomes shallower as the rate decreases.

questions.question: In the fermentation of glucose, a total of 960 mL of $\text{CO}_2$ gas was collected under standard laboratory conditions (25 °C and 100 kPa; molar volume 24.79 L mol$^{-1}$). Calculate the mass of ethanol produced in this reaction. Include a relevant equation in your answer.
questions.answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6(aq)\rightarrow2\text{CO}_2(g)+2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(aq)$. $n(\text{CO}_2)=\dfrac{0.960}{24.79}=0.03872$ mol. $n(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH})=n(\text{CO}_2)=0.03872$ mol. $m=0.03872\times46.07=1.78$ g.

questions.question: 25.00 mL of a straight chain gaseous hydrocarbon was reacted with 200.0 mL of oxygen at 25 °C. On cooling to 25 °C, the residual mixture of gases had a volume of 137.5 mL. This was shaken with potassium hydroxide solution to remove the carbon dioxide, dropping the final gas volume to 37.50 mL, consisting of oxygen only. Show your relevant working to identify the hydrocarbon.
questions.answer: $V(\text{CO}_2)=137.5-37.5=100.0$ mL. $V(\text{O}_2\text{ used})=200.0-37.5=162.5$ mL. By Gay-Lussac's law, volumes of gases at the same conditions are in the ratio of moles, so $\text{C}_x\text{H}_y:\text{O}_2:\text{CO}_2=25:162.5:100=1:6.5:4$. So $x=4$ and the equation is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}+6.5\text{O}_2\rightarrow4\text{CO}_2+5\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (oxygen balance: $2\times4+y/2=13$, so $y=10$). The hydrocarbon is butane, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$.

questions.question: Give the structural formula of 2,4-dimethylpentan-3-one.
questions.answer: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH-CO-CH(CH}_3)_2$: a five-carbon chain with a carbonyl group ($\text{C=O}$) on carbon 3 and a methyl group on each of carbons 2 and 4.

questions.question: Outline the information that could be obtained about 2,4-dimethylpentan-3-one using infrared spectroscopy.
questions.answer: Infrared spectroscopy gives information on the functional groups present. It would show a strong peak for the $\text{C=O}$ stretch at about $1680$–$1750\ \text{cm}^{-1}$, identifying a ketone (and no broad O–H peak).

questions.question: Describe the information that could be obtained about 2,4-dimethylpentan-3-one using carbon-13 NMR spectroscopy.
questions.answer: Carbon-13 NMR shows the number of different carbon environments and the types of carbon. A signal at about $190$–$220$ ppm would identify the carbonyl carbon of a ketone. It also shows the symmetry in the molecule: although the molecule has 7 carbon atoms, there would be only 3 signals (the carbonyl carbon, the two equivalent CH carbons, and the four equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ carbons).

questions.question: The pH in swimming pools is maintained between 7.2 and 7.8, commonly by adding sodium hydrogen carbonate at regular intervals. Which physical property of solid sodium hydrogen carbonate makes it suitable for use in swimming pool water?
questions.answer: It is highly soluble in water.

questions.question: Define the role of a buffer in an aqueous environment.
questions.answer: A buffer is a soluble chemical system (usually a weak acid and its conjugate base) that resists a change in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added, so that the solution stays within a narrow pH range.

questions.question: Justify the use of sodium hydrogen carbonate as a suitable buffer in swimming pools. Provide relevant chemical equations to support your answer.
questions.answer:
Sodium hydrogen carbonate dissolves to give the hydrogen carbonate ion, $\text{HCO}_3^-$, which is amphiprotic: it can act as a weak acid or a weak base (and sits in equilibrium with carbonate and carbonic acid), so it can neutralise small additions of acid or base and keep the pH constant (in accordance with Le Chatelier's principle).

When acid is added: $\text{HCO}_3^-(aq)+\text{H}^+(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)+\text{CO}_2(aq)$.

When base is added: $\text{HCO}_3^-(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)+\text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq)$.

These reactions maintain the pH within the range 7.2–7.8, minimising skin and eye irritation for swimmers.

questions.question: A $0.100\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ ammonium chloride solution has a pH of 4.60. What is the $K_a$ of this weak acid ($\text{NH}_4^+$)?
questions.answer: $\text{NH}_4^+(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{NH}_3(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$. $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=10^{-4.60}=2.51\times10^{-5}$ M. ICE: initial $[\text{NH}_4^+]=0.100$, $[\text{NH}_3]=[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=0$; change $-s,+s,+s$ with $s=2.51\times10^{-5}$; equilibrium $[\text{NH}_4^+]=0.100-2.51\times10^{-5}\approx0.100$, $[\text{NH}_3]=[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=2.51\times10^{-5}$. $K_a=\dfrac{[\text{NH}_3][\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]}{[\text{NH}_4^+]}=\dfrac{(2.51\times10^{-5})^2}{0.100}=6.3\times10^{-9}$.

questions.question: A $0.100\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ ammonium chloride solution has a pH of 4.60. What is the percent ionisation of the acid ($\text{NH}_4^+$)?
questions.answer: $\%\text{ionisation}=\dfrac{[\text{NH}_3]}{[\text{NH}_4^+]_{initial}}\times100=\dfrac{2.51\times10^{-5}}{0.100}\times100=0.0251\%$.

questions.question: The $K_a$ of the ammonium ion is $6.3\times10^{-9}$. Calculate its $pK_a$.

A primary straight chained alcohol, a carboxylic acid and an ester made with methanol are colourless liquids with molar masses of $88\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. Identify the compounds and explain the results of physical and chemical tests that could be performed to distinguish between the three liquids.
questions.answer:
The compounds: the alcohol is pentan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{OH}$ ($M=88.15$); the carboxylic acid is butanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ ($M=88.11$); the ester made with methanol is methyl propanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_3$ ($M=88.11$).

Physical tests: Boiling points. Methyl propanoate has the lowest, because it has no O–H group, so only dipole–dipole and dispersion forces act between molecules. Pentan-1-ol is higher as it has dispersion forces and hydrogen bonding. Butanoic acid has the highest because its molecules form more extensive (stronger) hydrogen bonding, needing the most energy to overcome. (Observed boiling points: methyl propanoate about $80^\circ\text{C}$, pentan-1-ol about $138^\circ\text{C}$, butanoic acid about $164^\circ\text{C}$.) Solubility in water: butanoic acid is completely miscible (polar, hydrogen bonds with water); pentan-1-ol is only slightly soluble, as the hydroxyl group hydrogen bonds with water but the longer non-polar chain limits solubility; the ester is insoluble and forms a layer above the water (and has a fruity smell).

Chemical tests: add acidified permanganate ($\text{H}^+/\text{MnO}_4^-$): the primary alcohol is oxidised (to a carboxylic acid), decolourising the purple permanganate, while the acid and ester do not react. Add sodium carbonate or hydrogen carbonate solution: only the carboxylic acid reacts, producing bubbles of $\text{CO}_2$ gas, while the alcohol and ester do not.

questions.question: Solutions 1–6 were prepared to produce a standard curve for $\text{Ni(NH}_3)_6^{2+}$, with volumes of $0.0010\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ of 0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0 and 5.0 mL, 5.0 mL of $4.0\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ $\text{NH}_3$ in each, and 5.0, 4.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0 and 0 mL of water respectively. Explain the purpose of the water in solutions 1–5.
questions.answer: The water makes the total volume of each of the six solutions 10.0 mL. This means the $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ concentration increases in regular amounts across the solutions, while the concentration of $\text{NH}_3$ stays identical in each solution (2.0 M), so that the concentration of the complex ion depends only on the volume of $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ added, and the absorbance readings can be validly compared.

questions.question: The complex ion forms in $\text{Ni}^{2+}(aq)+6\text{NH}_3(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ni(NH}_3)_6^{2+}(aq)$. A standard curve of absorbance against $[\text{Ni(NH}_3)_6^{2+}]$ is provided (absorbance 0, 0.04, 0.08, 0.12, 0.16 and 0.20 at concentrations $0$ to $5\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ in steps of $1\times10^{-4}$). The student made a new solution using 1.0 mL of $0.0070\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ $\text{Ni}^{2+}(aq)$, 1.0 mL of $0.40\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ $\text{NH}_3$ and 8.0 mL of water. An absorbance of 0.17 was recorded. Calculate the value of $K_{eq}$ for the complexation reaction.
questions.answer: Dilution (total volume 10.0 mL): initial $[\text{Ni}^{2+}]=0.0070\times\dfrac{1}{10}=7.0\times10^{-4}$ M and $[\text{NH}_3]=0.40\times\dfrac{1}{10}=0.040$ M. From the standard curve, an absorbance of 0.17 corresponds to $[\text{Ni(NH}_3)_6^{2+}]=4.25\times10^{-4}$ M (accept 4.2–4.3 $\times10^{-4}$). ICE: $[\text{Ni}^{2+}]=7.0\times10^{-4}-4.25\times10^{-4}=2.75\times10^{-4}$ M; $[\text{NH}_3]=0.040-6(4.25\times10^{-4})=0.0375$ M. $K_{eq}=\dfrac{[\text{Ni(NH}_3)_6^{2+}]}{[\text{Ni}^{2+}][\text{NH}_3]^6}=\dfrac{4.25\times10^{-4}}{(2.75\times10^{-4})(0.0375)^6}=5.6\times10^{8}$.

questions.question: For the complexation reaction $\text{Ni}^{2+}(aq)+6\text{NH}_3(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ni(NH}_3)_6^{2+}(aq)$ with $K_{eq}\gg1$: in making the standard curve, the student treated the reaction as having gone to completion with $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ as the limiting reagent (ammonia concentration 2.0 M, $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ at most $5\times10^{-4}$ M). When determining the unknown $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ in the later solution (ammonia only 0.040 M, $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ $7\times10^{-4}$ M), the system was treated as an equilibrium. Account for the two different treatments.
questions.answer: $K_{eq}=\dfrac{[\text{complex}]}{[\text{Ni}^{2+}][\text{NH}_3]^6}$, so $\dfrac{[\text{complex}]}{[\text{Ni}^{2+}]}=K_{eq}[\text{NH}_3]^6$. In the standard curve solutions the ammonia concentration was very high (at least 1.997 M, more than 4000 times that of nickel), so $[\text{NH}_3]^6$ is large, the ratio $[\text{complex}]/[\text{Ni}^{2+}]$ is huge, and the equilibrium lies so far to the right that essentially all of the $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ is complexed, so assuming completion is reasonable. In the second experiment the ammonia concentration was much lower (0.040 M, only about 57 times the nickel concentration), and since it is less than 1 M, $[\text{NH}_3]^6$ is tiny ($\approx2.8\times10^{-9}$ here, and the ratio is about 1.5, not $\gg1$), so the position of equilibrium is not as far right and not all of the nickel was complexed. An equilibrium (ICE table) treatment was therefore needed.

questions.question: An investigation used a series of precipitation reactions to determine the concentration of magnesium, silver and copper ions in a sample solution. A 25.0 mL aliquot was reacted with hydrochloric acid until no more precipitate formed; the precipitate was filtered and dried to a mass of 1.36 g. The filtrate was neutralised with dilute ammonia, and sodium hydroxide was added until no more precipitate formed; the mixture of blue and white precipitates, filtered and dried, had a mass of 2.40 g. In a separate experiment, a 20.0 mL aliquot of the sample was titrated with $0.427\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ sodium carbonate; a pale yellow silver precipitate formed first, then a blue copper precipitate, then a white magnesium precipitate. The titre volume was recorded once the white precipitate began to form: 41.10, 39.75, 39.85 and 39.80 mL. Calculate the concentrations of magnesium, silver and copper ions in the original sample solution. Include a relevant chemical equation for each precipitation reaction.
questions.answer:
Silver (HCl step): $\text{Ag}^+(aq)+\text{Cl}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{AgCl}(s)$. $n(\text{AgCl})=\dfrac{1.36}{143.35}=9.49\times10^{-3}$ mol $=n(\text{Ag}^+)$; $[\text{Ag}^+]=\dfrac{9.49\times10^{-3}}{0.0250}=0.380\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

Copper (carbonate titration; discard the outlier 41.10 mL): average titre $=\dfrac{39.75+39.85+39.80}{3}=39.80$ mL. $2\text{Ag}^+(aq)+\text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq)\rightarrow\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3(s)$ and $\text{Cu}^{2+}(aq)+\text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq)\rightarrow\text{CuCO}_3(s)$. $n(\text{CO}_3^{2-})=0.427\times0.03980=0.01700$ mol. In the 20.0 mL aliquot, $n(\text{Ag}^+)=0.380\times0.0200=7.59\times10^{-3}$ mol, which uses $\dfrac{7.59\times10^{-3}}{2}=3.80\times10^{-3}$ mol of carbonate. $n(\text{Cu}^{2+})=0.01700-0.00380=0.01320$ mol, so $[\text{Cu}^{2+}]=\dfrac{0.01320}{0.0200}=0.660\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

Magnesium (hydroxide precipitate, 25.0 mL aliquot): $\text{Cu}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{Cu(OH)}_2(s)$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{Mg(OH)}_2(s)$. $n(\text{Cu}^{2+})=0.660\times0.0250=0.0165$ mol, $m(\text{Cu(OH)}_2)=0.0165\times97.57=1.61$ g. $m(\text{Mg(OH)}_2)=2.40-1.61=0.79$ g, $n=\dfrac{0.79}{58.33}=0.0135$ mol $=n(\text{Mg}^{2+})$. $[\text{Mg}^{2+}]=\dfrac{0.0135}{0.0250}=0.54\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

questions.question: The following information was obtained from the analysis of an unknown organic compound. Chemical reactivity: $\text{NaHCO}_3(aq)$ gave bubbling; $\text{H}^+/\text{KMnO}_4(aq)$ stayed a dark magenta solution; $\text{Br}_2(aq)$ gave a colourless solution. Mass spectrum: molecular ion at $m/z$ 114, base peak at $m/z$ 69, other peaks at about 43, 45, 71, 97 and 99. Proton NMR: singlet, 1 H, about 11 ppm; triplet, 1 H, about 7.2 ppm; doublet, 1 H, about 6.0 ppm; octet, 1 H, about 2.7 ppm; doublet, 6 H, about 1.2 ppm. Give the structural formula for the unknown compound that is consistent with all the information provided. Justify your structure with reference to the relevant information from each source of data.
questions.answer:
The compound is 4-methylpent-2-enoic acid, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH-CH=CH-COOH}$ ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2$).

Chemical reactivity: bubbles with $\text{NaHCO}_3$ show an acid ($\text{CO}_2$ is released), so there is a carboxylic acid group. Bromine water is decolourised by an addition reaction, showing a $\text{C=C}$ double bond is present. (The school's solution reads the unchanged magenta colour of acidified permanganate as showing no alcohol or aldehyde is present; note that an alkene would normally also decolourise permanganate, so this observation is not consistent with an alkene, and the bromine test is the evidence for the double bond.)

Mass spectrum: the molecular ion at $m/z=114$ gives the molar mass. $\text{COOH}$ has mass 45, leaving 69 for the carbon chain. The 10 hydrogens in the NMR, less 1 for the acid group, leave 9 H on the chain, and the chain is $\text{C}_5\text{H}_9$ ($60+9=69$), which includes the double bond. The base peak at 69 is $[(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH=CH}]^+$ (loss of $\text{COOH}$); 71 is $[\text{CH=CHCOOH}]^+$; 97 is loss of OH ($[(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH=CHCO}]^+$); 99 is loss of $\text{CH}_3$; 43 is $[(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}]^+$; and 45 is $[\text{COOH}]^+$.

Proton NMR: the 1 H singlet at about 11 ppm is the carboxylic acid proton, with no neighbouring hydrogens. The 6 H doublet at about 1.2 ppm is two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ groups, each next to one H (the CH). That CH is the 1 H octet at about 2.7 ppm (split by 6 H from the two methyls plus 1 H from the alkene CH, so $n+1=8$). The alkene H next to it is the signal at about 7.2 ppm (1 H) and the other alkene H (next to COOH) is at about 6.0 ppm (1 H, doublet because it is next to only one H). This gives the fragments $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH-}$, $-\text{CH=CH-}$ and $-\text{COOH}$ joined in order.

questions.question: Discuss the effects of enthalpy and entropy in the reaction between octane and oxygen in a flame.
questions.answer:
The reaction is $2\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18}(l)+25\text{O}_2(g)\rightarrow16\text{CO}_2(g)+18\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$ (the water is a gas in the flame, as the temperature is above $100^\circ\text{C}$).

Enthalpy: combustion is highly exothermic ($\Delta H<0$): the stronger bonds formed in the products release more energy than is needed to break the bonds in the reactants, and the energy is released as heat (and light), which favours the reaction.

Entropy: there are 25 mol of gas in the reactants (plus liquid octane) and 34 mol of gas in the products, so the number of gas particles increases, the dispersal of matter and energy increases and $\Delta S>0$, which also favours the reaction.

$\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S$: with $\Delta H<0$ and $\Delta S>0$, $\Delta G$ is negative at all temperatures, so the reaction is spontaneous. (A spark or flame is needed only to provide the activation energy to start the reaction, not because it is non-spontaneous.)

questions.question: The forward reaction in the equilibrium $\text{OCl}^{-}$(aq) + $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$(l) ⇌ $\text{HOCl}$(aq) + $\text{OH}^{-}$(aq) is endothermic. Which change increases the concentration of the hypochlorous acid ($\text{HOCl}$)?
questions.answer: Adding $\text{NaOCl}$ increases $\text{OCl}^{-}$, so the equilibrium shifts right (Le Chatelier) and $\text{HOCl}$ increases (B). Water is a liquid, so adding it does not change the position; adding $\text{OH}^{-}$ shifts the equilibrium left; lowering the temperature shifts it left (the forward reaction is endothermic).

questions.question: 0.1 moles of each of the following substances is dissolved in 1 L of water. For which substance would the pH of the solution be the closest to 14?
questions.answer: $\text{Ca(OH)}_{2}$ is a strong base giving two $\text{OH}^{-}$ per formula unit, so $[\text{OH}^-]$ = 0.2 M, pOH = 0.70 and pH ≈ 13.3 (A). Ethanol is neutral, $\text{NH}_{4}\text{Cl}$ is acidic and $\text{NaCH}_{3}\text{COO}$ is only weakly basic.

questions.question: A saturated solution of $\text{BaSO}_{4}$ is maintained at constant temperature. Solid soluble $\text{Na}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ is added to this solution. What happens to the $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ ion concentrations in the resultant solution compared to the initial solution?
questions.answer: Common ion effect: $\text{Na}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ dissolves completely and raises $[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]$, so the equilibrium $\text{BaSO}_{4}$(s) ⇌ $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ + $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ shifts left. Some $\text{BaSO}_{4}$ precipitates, so $[\text{Ba}^{2+}]$ falls, but the total $[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]$ ends higher than before, because $K_{sp}$ is constant (C).
options: $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ concentration increases and $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ concentration remains the same
$\text{Ba}^{2+}$ concentration decreases and $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ concentration remains the same

questions.question: The graph shows the changes in pH during a titration. Which indicator should be chosen for this titration?
questions.answer: The pH starts at about 14 (a strong base in the flask) and falls steeply between about pH 12 and pH 6, to a weakly acidic final pH of about 5. The indicator's range must lie within the steep section: phenolphthalein (8.3–10.0) changes colour entirely within it (D). Methyl orange and bromocresol green change below the vertical section and would give a gradual, unclear end-point.

questions.question: Which of these substances is an example of a polyprotic acid?
questions.answer: A polyprotic acid can donate more than one proton per molecule. $\text{HCl}$, $\text{HNO}_{3}$ and $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH}$ each donate one proton (monoprotic). Only the option with three ionisable hydrogen atoms, $\text{H}_{3}\text{CrO}_{4}$, is polyprotic (C).

questions.question: Below is an equation for a reversible reaction: 2$\text{CrO}_{4}^{2-}$(aq) + 2$\text{H}^{+}$(aq) ⇌ $\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-}$(aq) + $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$(l). The reaction's correct equilibrium expression is:
questions.answer: $K=\dfrac{[\text{products}]}{[\text{reactants}]}$ with each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient. Pure liquid water is omitted (its concentration is constant). So $K=\dfrac{[\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}]}{[\text{CrO}_4^{2-}]^2[\text{H}^+]^2}$ (B).

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of the following compound? The six-carbon chain CH3-CH2-CHCl-CHCl-CHF-CH3 has chlorine atoms on the third and fourth carbons from the left, and a fluorine on the fifth carbon from the left (that is, the carbon next to the end carbon on the right).
questions.answer: Number the chain so that the substituents have the lowest set of locants: from the right they are at 2, 3, 4 (from the left they would be 3, 4, 5). Substituents are listed alphabetically (chloro before fluoro) with the multiplier 'di' for the two chlorines: 3,4-dichloro-2-fluorohexane (D).

questions.question: Chlorine gas ($\text{Cl}_{2}$) and carbon monoxide gas (CO) are placed in a sealed container and kept at a temperature of 25 °C. Phosgene gas is produced as follows: $\text{Cl}_{2}$(g) + CO(g) ⇌ $\text{COCl}_{2}$(g). Which statements about this reaction are correct?
questions.answer: In a closed system the reaction reaches dynamic equilibrium: the forward and reverse rates become equal, so the concentrations (including $\text{COCl}_{2}$) stop changing (D). A is wrong because the reaction is reversible and does not go to completion. C is wrong because the forward reaction does not stop at equilibrium; it continues, balanced by the reverse reaction.
options: All the $\text{Cl}_{2}$ and CO will be converted into $\text{COCl}_{2}$
At a temperature of 25 °C the $\text{COCl}_{2}$ will not form
The forward reaction will continue to occur until the concentration of $\text{COCl}_{2}$ remains constant
When the forward and reverse reactions become equal the concentration of $\text{COCl}_{2}$ becomes constant

questions.question: The molar masses of $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{6}$, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$ and $\text{CH}_{3}\text{F}$ are similar. Which of the following lists these compounds in order of increasing boiling point?
questions.answer: $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{6}$ is non-polar (dispersion forces only), so it has the lowest boiling point. $\text{CH}_{3}\text{F}$ is polar (dipole–dipole forces) and cannot hydrogen bond. $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$ has an O–H group and forms hydrogen bonds, the strongest of the three, so it has the highest boiling point (B).

questions.question: The diagram shows molecules P and Q reacting to form R and water. P is HCOOH (methanoic acid), Q is CH3NH2 and R is HCONHCH3. Which row of the table correctly identifies the molecule types?
questions.answer: P has a –COOH group (carboxylic acid), Q has an –NH₂ group on an alkyl group (a primary amine), and R has the –CONH– linkage (an amide), formed by a condensation reaction releasing water (A).
options: P: carboxylic acid; Q: amine; R: amide
P: carboxylic acid; Q: amide; R: amine
P: alcohol; Q: amine; R: ester
P: aldehyde; Q: amide; R: ketone

questions.question: The spectrum of visible light, structural formula and UV absorption spectrum of methylbenzene is shown. Based on the information, which statement about methylbenzene is correct?
questions.answer: The absorbance spectrum peaks at about 290 nm and is almost zero above about 350 nm, so methylbenzene absorbs in the ultraviolet and does not absorb any visible light (400–700 nm). All visible wavelengths are transmitted, so a solution appears colourless (A). The spectrum starts at 200 nm, so it says nothing about wavelengths below 100 nm.
options: A solution of methylbenzene would appear colourless
A solution of methylbenzene would appear as an orange-red colour
Methylbenzene only absorbs in the visible part of the electromagnetic spectrum
Methylbenzene does not absorb wavelengths lower than 100 nm

questions.question: The graph refers to the gaseous reaction aA(g) + bB(g) ⇌ cC(g) + dD(g). The effect of increasing pressure and temperature on the equilibrium yield of products is shown in the graph. Which of the following alternatives regarding the equilibrium systems is consistent with the data?
questions.answer: The yield of product increases as the pressure increases, so the forward reaction reduces the number of moles of gas: a + b > c + d. The yield decreases as the temperature increases (the 350 °C curve is the highest), so the forward reaction is exothermic, ΔH < 0 (C).
options: a + b < c + d, ΔH negative
a + b < c + d, ΔH positive
a + b > c + d, ΔH negative
a + b > c + d, ΔH positive

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of compounds will form a precipitate when 0.1 mol L⁻¹ solutions of each are mixed?
questions.answer: All nitrates are soluble, and so are all potassium, sodium and bromide salts of these metals, so A, B (copper(II) sulfate is soluble) and C produce no precipitate. In D, $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ form insoluble copper(II) hydroxide: $\text{Cu}^{2+}$(aq) + 2$\text{OH}^{-}$(aq) → $\text{Cu(OH)}_{2}$(s) (D).

questions.question: A student performed a titration to determine the concentration of an unknown sodium hydroxide solution using a standard solution of hydrochloric acid. They performed the following steps: a burette was rinsed with deionised water, then rinsed again with the sodium hydroxide solution; the burette was then filled with the sodium hydroxide solution; a volumetric pipette and a conical flask were both washed with deionised water, then washed again with the hydrochloric acid solution; 25 mL of the hydrochloric acid solution was transferred into the conical flask using the pipette and an appropriate indicator added; the titration was performed until the end-point, and the titrant volume recorded. The calculated concentration based on the method described above will be:
questions.answer: Rinsing the burette with NaOH and the pipette with HCl is correct. Rinsing the conical flask with HCl is not: the residual acid adds extra moles of HCl to the 25 mL taken, so more NaOH is needed to reach the end-point and the titre is larger than it should be. The calculated concentration ($c_{\text{NaOH}}$ = n(HCl)/titre, using only the 25 mL pipetted) is therefore lower than the true value (B).
options: The same as the true value
Different than the true value, but there is insufficient information to determine if it would be higher or lower

questions.question: Four organic compounds are identified by the numbers I, II, III, IV: I – $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$; II – $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$; III – $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}$; IV – $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$. Which alternative identifies the strongest acid and strongest base in the list?
questions.answer: The carboxylic acid (I) is by far the strongest acid of the four (ethanol and the amide are neutral, the amine is basic). The amine (IV) has a lone pair on nitrogen that readily accepts a proton, while in the amide (III) the lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl group and the amide is essentially neutral. So the strongest acid is I and the strongest base is IV (B).
options: Strongest acid I, strongest base III
Strongest acid I, strongest base IV
Strongest acid II, strongest base III
Strongest acid II, strongest base IV

questions.question: The diagram shows a polymer (a carbon chain with a –CONH₂ group on every second carbon). Identify the type of polymerisation reaction used to produce it and the monomer or monomer units used to make it.
questions.answer: The backbone consists only of carbon–carbon single bonds, with a –CONH₂ side group on every second carbon, and no small molecule is lost. This is an addition polymer made from the alkene monomer CH₂=CH–CONH₂ (prop-2-enamide, acrylamide) (A). The side groups are single, not alternating with –CH₃ groups, so B is wrong, and a condensation polymer would contain linkages such as amide bonds in the backbone.
options: Condensation, from ethene and carbamic acid, H2N–COOH (two monomers)
Condensation, from two molecules of carbamic acid, H2N–COOH

questions.question: What is the function of the hollow cathode lamp in an atomic absorption spectrometer?
questions.answer: The cathode of the lamp is made of the element being analysed, so the lamp emits the characteristic wavelengths of that element. These are absorbed by the free gaseous atoms of that element in the flame (A). The flame, not the lamp, atomises the sample.
options: Provide a specific wavelength of light that can be absorbed by free atoms in the gaseous state
Separate molecules in the tested sample so that free atoms are formed
Convert free atoms in the tested sample into gaseous ions
Produce a frequency of light that is absorbed by particular bonds of molecules in the sample being tested

questions.question: The graph shows the concentrations over time for the equilibrium system 2$\text{NO}_{2}$(g) ⇌ $\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{4}$(g), ΔH = −58 kJ mol⁻¹. What has happened to the temperature at T₁ and to the volume at T₂?
questions.answer: At T₁ the concentrations change gradually (no sudden jump), so the change is a temperature change. $\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{4}$ decreases and $\text{NO}_{2}$ increases, so the equilibrium shifts left, favouring the endothermic reverse reaction: the temperature increased. At T₂ both concentrations drop suddenly, so the volume increased (concentrations fall). Then $\text{NO}_{2}$ rises and $\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{4}$ falls, a shift to the side with more moles of gas (2 mol of $\text{NO}_{2}$ against 1 mol of $\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{4}$), consistent with a decrease in pressure (D).
options: Temperature decreased at T₁ and volume increased at T₂
Temperature increased at T₁ and volume decreased at T₂
Temperature decreased at T₁ and volume decreased at T₂
Temperature increased at T₁ and volume increased at T₂

questions.question: A researcher was examining a sample of the polymer polyvinyl chloride (PVC) to determine its chain length. The sample was found to have a molar mass of 623 800 g mol⁻¹. A section of the chain is shown (the repeating unit –CH₂–CHCl–). What is the value of n?

1.23 g of a pure acid, $\text{H}_{2}\text{X}$(s), is added to exactly 250.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH(aq): $\text{H}_{2}\text{X}$(s) + 2NaOH(aq) → $\text{Na}_{2}\text{X}$(aq) + 2$\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$(l). The NaOH is in excess. This excess NaOH requires 27.50 mL of 0.20 M HCl(aq) for neutralisation. What is the molar mass of the acid?
questions.answer: n(NaOH) added $=0.100\times0.2500=0.02500$ mol. n(excess NaOH) $=n(\text{HCl})=0.20\times0.02750=0.00550$ mol. n(NaOH) reacted $=0.01950$ mol. n($\text{H}_2\text{X}$) $=\tfrac12(0.01950)=0.00975$ mol. $M=\dfrac{1.23}{0.00975}=126$ g mol⁻¹ (D).
